03_marg71: He did not say “In the beginning God said: Let heaven and earth be made,” but he said “Be light made, and light was made,” because by the name of heaven and earth was to be comprehended in general whatever God made. Then it was to be set out part by part how he made it. Whence there follows: “God said: Be … made,” that is, he made it through his Word. Or because, when unformed matter, spiritual or bodily, was first being made, it was not to be said “God said: Be … made.” For it was unfitting for “Be made” to be said by God, because imperfection does not imitate the form of the Word except by the conversion of its kind to the Creator. The creature is made perfect, so that when it is said “God said: Be … made,” we understand that he calls the imperfection of the creature back to himself. So when it is said “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” mention is made of the Son, because he is the beginning. But when it is said “God said: Be … made,” he is mentioned because he is the Word. By “beginning” he marks the start of the creature existing from him; by “Word,” the perfecting of the creature called back from him to himself, so that it may be formed by imitating the unchangeable form of the Word. For the Word of God, for whom to be is to live, indeed to live is the same as to live blessedly, has no unformed life. But the spiritual creature has an unformed life, for which to be is not the same as to live, nor to live the same as to live blessedly; because, turned away from the wisdom of God, it lives foolishly and wretchedly.
03_marg72: Scripture, making known the creation of the world, shows by its first word the eternity and omnipotence of God. For him whom it says created the world in the beginning of times, it signifies to have existed eternally before times; and him whom it tells created heaven and earth at the start of the founding, it declares to be almighty with such speed of working that for him to have willed is to have made. So it is well said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” namely both together, although both are not said together by man. Whence the prophet shows the earth made in the beginning, saying: “In the beginning, O Lord, thou foundedst the earth,” etc.
03_marg73: The heaven: not the visible firmament but the empyrean, that is, the fiery or intellectual heaven, which is so called not from burning but from brightness; which was at once filled with angels. Whence in Job: “Where wast thou when the morning stars praised me,” etc. And note that three elements are mentioned here. By the name of heaven we understand the air; by the name of earth, the earth itself and the fire that lies hidden in it. Mention of the fourth, that is, water, is made in what follows.
03_marg74: In the beginning. ALCUIN. In the Son; when he was made man it became plain who were heavenly and who earthly.
03_marg75: Heaven: the spiritual creature, perfect and blessed from the start. Earth: bodily matter, still imperfect.
03_marg76: The unformed matter of spiritual life, as it can exist in itself, not turned to the Creator, in whom it is formed. The bodily earth without any of the qualities that appear in formed matter.
03_marg77: Scripture says: “who madest the world of matter without form.” The matter was made from nothing; the form of the world from unformed matter.
03_marg78: Bede: So God made two things before all time: the angelic creature and unformed matter; although Solomon says: “He that liveth for ever created all things together.” Yet according to Origen, unformed matter goes before the formed appearance. So God made the world and the angels and the soul from nothing; man and the other creatures from something.
03_marg79: There are seven heavens, whose names are these: the air, the ether, Olympus, space, and the fiery firmament, the heaven of the angels and that of the Trinity. But Jerome says the heaven of the Trinity is the first; the second, that of the angels; the third, the firmament.
03_marg80: And earth: mystically. “In the beginning God created heaven and earth”: namely those who bore the image of the heavenly, and the earth, that is, those who afterwards by pride made themselves misshapen, bearing the earth, that is, the image of the earthly man. The earth was void, because it had laid aside the good form; and empty of the fruit of good work; and darkness, namely the lack of the true light, was upon the face of the deep, namely the hearts of the proud.

03_marg81: And the earth was void and empty. BEDE. He shows what, or what kind of, heaven was made in the beginning with the earth. For he adds this about the earth, which he wished to be understood of the heaven. For this upper heaven, which is set apart from the turning of the world, as soon as it was created was filled with the holy angels, whom the Lord bears witness were made in the beginning with heaven and earth, saying: “Where wast thou when the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?” He calls the same angels morning stars and sons of God. For of the heaven in which the lights are set, how or when was it made? He says afterwards.
03_marg82: But the earth was void and empty: that is, useless and fruitless and unordered. For all the elements were mixed and confused, and this whole space of the air was full of waters, not such as they are now, but like thin clouds, such as those above the heavens still are.
03_interl15: it signifies the spiritual nature, which, turned to the Creator, is formed and enlightened
03_interl16: because there was no light to be over it and poured over it
03_marg83: And darkness was upon the face of the deep. AUGUSTINE. Namely because there was no light, which, if it had been, would also have been over it and poured over it; which happens in the spiritual creature when it is turned to the unchangeable light, which is God.
03_marg84: Bede: Darkness was upon the face of the deep. Those are not to be heard who say, finding fault, that God created darkness before light, because he made no darkness in water or air; but by the distinct order of his providence he first created the waters with heaven and earth, and when he willed, he made them lovely with the grace of light. And it is to be noted that with the heaven two elements of the world were created, into which the other two were set: namely water and earth, in which are fire and air. And the waters covered the whole surface of the earth to such a height that they reached up to those places where even now they partly rest above the firmament. And the earth itself and the water are called unformed matter, because all things that we see took their beginning either from these or from nothing; and before they came into the light, there was nothing from which they might have form.
03_marg85: Augustine: historically. “And the spirit of God moved over the waters.” Either he called the whole bodily matter water, to suggest from what were made and formed all the things which we see formed on the earth in various kinds out of a moist nature; or the spiritual life, as it were flowing, before the form of its conversion. The Spirit of God moved over it, because what he had begun, to be formed and perfected, lay under the good will of the Creator. It is said also, “the spirit of the Lord moved over the waters,” lest God should be thought to love his works by making them from the necessity of need rather than from the abundance of his goodness. For it is fittingly first suggested that something was begun over which he might move, not in place but by power surpassing all things.
03_interl19: the good will of the Creator, beneath which lay what was to be formed
03_interl21: in the Syrian tongue: he brooded over it, as a bird its eggs
03_interl22: as the wisdom of the craftsman moves over the work to be made
03_interl24: the whole bodily frame of things, because the things we see are formed into various kinds out of a moist nature
03_interl25: or the spiritual life, as it were flowing, before the form of its conversion
03_marg86: And the spirit of God moved over the waters. JEROME. In the Hebrew it has merephet, that is, “brooded” or “cherished,” in the manner of a bird warming its eggs with the heat of a living body. So we understand it said not of the spirit of the world, as many think, but of the Holy Spirit, who himself also gives life to all things. And if he gives life, he is the maker; if the maker, he is God. For “Send forth,” it says, “thy spirit, and they shall be created.”
03_marg87: And the spirit: in whom we might rest, standing firm, made alive by his breath and washed by the wave of baptism.
03_marg88: And the spirit of God moved over the waters: namely as God and maker, he was over the flowing and confused matter, to set it apart when he willed. So the whole Trinity is understood to have worked here: God, namely the Father; the Beginning, the Son; the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit.
03_marg89: And the spirit. ISIDORE. Mystically. Namely the wavering hearts which had lost the quiet of the mind, because the Spirit did not rest upon them but moved over them, as one able to call them back from confusion to better things. Then through the whole text of this Scripture we see six ages of labour, as it were, though marked off by bounds close to one another, so that in the seventh rest may be hoped for; and that they bear a likeness to the six days in which were made the things Scripture records God to have made.
03_marg90: Over the waters: for the beginning of the human race, in which it began to enjoy this light, is compared to the first day, in which God made light. This age is as it were the infancy of the whole world, which we think of as one man, in proportion to its greatness. For man, when he is first born into the light, passes through infancy, the first age, which stretches from Adam to Noe through ten generations. The flood is as it were the evening of this day, because our infancy is blotted out by the flood of forgetfulness.

03_marg91: Said. ALCUIN. He put the perfect tense to show the speed or ease of God’s work.
03_marg92: God said: Be light made. The light made on the first day is understood as spiritual or bodily.
03_marg93: And light was made: if spiritual, not that light coeternal with the Father through which all things were made, but that of which it is said, “Wisdom hath been created before all things,” that is, the intellectual and angelic life, which flows formlessly unless turned to the Creator; which can be the first creature, and was called heaven when it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” but turned to the Creator when it is said, “Be light made, and light was made.” In which spiritual light perhaps the dividing of the light from the darkness is understood as the setting apart of the thing already formed from the unformed. The naming of day and night is the sign of the distribution by which it is signified that God leaves nothing disordered, and that the advances of creatures are not without the filling-up of the beauty of the whole. The evening, in the three days before the lights were made, is the end of the finished work; the morning, the beginning of the one to come. But if bodily light was made on the first day, the adorning of the world fittingly begins with the light, by which the other things that were to be created were seen. And if it is asked where it was made, when the deep covered the whole height of the earth, it is plain: in those parts which the daily light of the sun now lights up. Nor is it a wonder that light can shine in waters, since they are often lit up even by the work of sailors who, plunged in the depths, light up the waters for themselves by oil let out from the mouth; and those waters were in the beginning much thinner than they are now, because they were not yet gathered into one place.
03_marg94: And God said: Be … made. AUGUSTINE. Historically, not in time. For if in time, then changeably; if changeably, then through a creature beneath him; if through a creature beneath him, light is not the first creature. But perhaps, because it had already been said, “In the beginning God made heaven,” etc., this voice, “Be light made,” could be made in time through the heavenly creature. If so, this bodily light was made through a creature beneath him which he had made before, when the Lord said, “Be light made.” How it could be said divinely through the hidden movement of the spiritual creature: for the voice of God did not sound bodily, as that one did: “Thou art my Son,” etc. For in what tongue would it sound, when there was not yet a diversity of tongues, nor was there one single tongue to speak it, nor anyone who had to hear and understand? So the voice of God is rightly taken as the Word, which is understood in the sound of the voice. For this very thing is said to belong to the nature of the Word through which all things were made. So what God said, “Be light made,” is eternal, because the Word of God is coeternal with the Father. For when we hear “And God said: Be … made,” we understand that it was in the Word that it should be made. And when he adds, “And it was made so,” we understand that the creature made did not go beyond the bounds of its kind fixed in the Word. And when it is said, “God saw that it was good,” we understand in the kindness of his Spirit not that it pleased him as though known after it was made, but that it pleased him to remain made in the same goodness in which it pleased him that it should be made. For God loves his creature so that it may be and may remain.
03_marg95: Be light made. AUGUSTINE. Historically. Namely by that condition by which all things subsist, timelessly in the wisdom of God before in themselves. “And light was made,” that is, the angelic and heavenly substance in itself in time, as it was eternally in wisdom as to its unchangeableness. Or the unformedness and imperfection of this creature, before it was formed in the love of its maker, is noted. For it is formed when it is turned to the unchangeable light of the Word.
03_marg96: AUGUSTINE. If bodily light was made, what then is that light which we cannot see when the sun has set, since neither the moon nor the stars existed? But perhaps it is in that part of heaven where the sun is: not the sun’s light, but so joined to it that it cannot be told apart. Or perhaps God had made the light in that part where he was going to make man, so that when the light had left that part it might be called evening. But why was the sun made to rule the day, if that light was enough to make the day? But perhaps the earlier light lit up only the higher parts, and for the lighting of the lower parts the sun had to be made. It can also be said that the brightness of the day was increased by the sun being added. But if we understand night and day as the sending-out and drawing-in of that light, what cause will be given? For there were not yet animals for whom this alternation would be shown.
03_interl34: that is, he willed it to be seen
03_interl35: that is, it pleased him in its own being, as it had first pleased him in his wisdom
03_marg97: And God saw the light, etc. AUGUSTINE. He did not praise the light as though unknown, but declared it, already made, worthy of praise. But because he did not drive out the whole darkness of the world with light, it is rightly added, “and he divided the light from the darkness”; for he divided them not only by difference of quality but also of place, spreading the light in the upper part while darkness remained in the lower. “And he called the light Day,” etc. This naming was made in no tongue, because with God there is pure understanding without the noise of a tongue. But “he called,” that is, he made it to be called, because he so distinguished them that they could be told apart and named.
03_interl36: that is, the sons of light
03_interl42: tenebrae (darkness) is named from tenendo (holding), for it holds the eyes
03_marg98: And he divided the light, etc. AUGUSTINE. This was done from the moment the light was made. But it could not be said by man all at once, as it was done by God. And the dividing of light from darkness is the distinction between the perfect state of each thing and the defect it has of itself. For we understand day in the form of the thing made, and night in its privation or defect, which is in things made in time of themselves, even if the effect is lacking. Evening in all things is the end of the perfect making; morning, the beginning of what is starting. For every creature is held within fixed beginnings and ends. For there were not yet solar days, so that the rising of the sun might be called day and its setting evening; which was done on the fourth day, when the lights were first set in order in the firmament.
03_marg99: Strabo: God made light and darkness. Whence: “O light and darkness, bless the Lord,” where every creature is invited to bless.
03_marg100: Isidore: otherwise. Each one has, in his works and right life, six distinct days, after which he may hope for rest. On the first day, the light of faith, when he first believes in things invisible; for the sake of which faith the Lord deigned to appear.

03_interl49: the first distinction of the divine works
03_marg101: And it is to be noted that the night in those three days was wholly dark, which, after the stars were created, shone with some light. It was fitting too that the days should begin from light and stretch to the morning of the following day, so that the works of God might be signified to have been begun from light and completed into light.
03_marg102: And there was evening, etc. GREGORY. Sin is by no means so left behind in this life through the exercise of justice that one remains in it unshaken; because even if uprightness drives out guilt, it sits at the doors of our thought and knocks that it may be opened to it. Whence Moses says: “Light was made,” and a little after: “there was evening.” For the Creator, foreknowing human guilt, then expressed in time what now turns about in the mind. For the shadow of temptation follows the light of uprightness. But because the light of the elect is not quenched by temptation, it is recorded that not night but evening was made; because temptation hides the light of justice, it does not kill it.
03_marg103: Augustine: it is to be noted that the other creatures which are beneath the spiritual light are not made without its knowledge (John). The same day is repeated everywhere, so that by its repetition there may be as many days as the kinds of created things are distinguished, to be ended in the perfection of the number six; namely so that the evening of the first day is its knowledge of itself: that it is not what God is. And the morning after this evening, by which the first day is closed and the second begun, is its turning, so that it refers its having been created to the praise of the Creator, and receives from the Word of God the knowledge of the creature made after it, that is, the firmament, which is first made in its knowledge through the Word, afterwards in the nature of the firmament itself. Then comes the evening of this light, when the firmament is known no longer in the Word of God, as before, but in the firmament’s own nature; which knowledge, because it is lesser, is called evening. After this comes the morning, by which the second is closed and the third begins. In which morning likewise is the turning of the light, that is, of this day, to praising God who made the firmament, and to receiving from his Word the knowledge of the creature to be made after the firmament; and so on to the morning after the evening of the sixth day. For there is a great difference between the knowledge of a thing in the Word of God and the knowledge of it in its nature: so that the former belongs to the day, the latter to the evening.

03_marg104: Amidst the waters: those hanging as vapour and those gliding over the earth.
03_marg105: God said: Let there be a firmament made amidst the waters … and there was evening. AUGUSTINE. As the light set little by little and, after the space of a day’s length, went under the lower parts, there was evening, as now happens in the usual round of the sun. And there was morning when the same returned over the earth and began another day; and one day of twenty-four hours was completed.
03_marg106: Let there be a firmament made, etc. GREGORY. The angelic powers that persevered in the love of God received this in reward: that they remain in the contemplation of their Creator in everlasting happiness, and subsist eternally in that in which they were made. Whence in Moses heaven is said to be made, and the same is afterwards called the firmament; because the angelic nature was first made subtle in the higher places, and afterwards more wonderfully made firm, so that it could never fall.
03_marg107: Let there be a firmament made, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether that heaven which is beyond the spaces of the air is now made, or whether the air itself is called the firmament. For they assert that waters cannot be above the starry heaven, since their weight requires that they flow above the earth or are carried as vapour in the air. Nor let anyone say that this is done by the omnipotence of God. For what is asked is how God made the natures of things, not what he might work in them miraculously by his power. And those who deny that waters can be above the heaven distinguish the elements not only by places but also by qualities, by which they are allotted their own places: so that water is above the earth, air above the water, heaven above the air. Whence it is gathered that if air remained above the heaven, it would fall by its weight, and so water cannot be above the heaven. Whence some try to show that the waters are above the heavens, taking the air here as heaven and firmament for this reason only, that its interval divides between certain vapours of the waters and the waters which are on the earth.
03_marg108: Let there be a firmament made, etc. AUGUSTINE. Historically. It is to be noted that the firmament is so called not because it stands still, but because of its firmness and the uncrossable bound between the upper and lower waters; whether we understand the airy heaven, or that which is beyond the spaces of the cloudy air, which by the breathing-out of the earth draws up waters as vapour and holds them up in fine particles, and afterwards, gathered into heavier balls, pours them back as rain. And if water can, as we see, come to such fine particles that it is carried as vapour above the air, which is naturally lighter than waters, why should we not believe that it may also flow over that lighter heaven in finer drops and lighter vapours? But in whatever way they are there, we do not doubt that they are there.
03_marg109: Bede: “Let there be a firmament made amidst,” etc. The creation of the heaven in which the stars are fixed is described, which is plainly amidst the waters. For waters are set beneath it, in the air and on the earth, and set above it, of which it is said: “Who coverest the higher rooms thereof with water.” So the firmament in the midst is the starry heaven, which can be believed to have been made of waters. For crystal, a stone of great firmness and great clearness, is made of waters. If anyone is troubled how waters, of a fluid nature and slipping downward, can stand above the heaven, whose shape seems to be round, let him remember that it is written of him: “He bindeth up the waters in his clouds.” For he who binds up waters beneath the heaven, held for a time in the vapours of the clouds, can hold up waters above the sphere of the heaven, lest they slip down, not with the thinness of vapour but with the solidity of ice; he who also hangs the mass of the earth upon nothing. But of what kind they are and for what use, he knows who made them.

03_interl57: the peoples of men, who need it

03_interl61: morally: so that through the firmament itself, namely of Scripture, he may distinguish between fleshly and spiritual things as between upper and lower waters
03_marg110: And God made a firmament, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why, when he had said “Let there be a firmament made, and it was so,” he afterwards added “And God made a firmament,” when this was not added in the creation of the light. In which it is shown that on the first day, on which the light was made, the making of the spiritual creature, that is, the holy angels, is signified by the light. Therefore it is not repeated after he said “light was made,” because the rational creature did not first know its forming and afterwards was formed, but knew it in its very forming. For the making of the light is in them first in wisdom, afterwards in their own making: there begotten, here made, that is, formed out of the unformed. Whence “Be light made, and light was made,” so that what was in the Word might be in the work. The other things are made first in wisdom, afterwards in the knowledge of the angels, at last in their own kind. So when we hear “God said: Be light made,” we understand Scripture’s going back to the wisdom of God. When we hear “it was made,” we understand that in the spiritual creature knowledge of the creature to be made was produced. When there is added “And God made,” we understand the very nature in its kind. Nor did God say “Be … made” as many times as Scripture says it, because he begot one Word, in which he said all things, through which each thing was made. But Scripture, coming down to the little ones, looks in each kind of creature to the eternal reason in the Word of God, saying: “God said: Be … made,” etc.
03_marg111: AUGUSTINE. Above the air the heaven is said to be pure fire. From which they conjecture that the stars and lights were made, namely the nature of that fiery light gathered into balls and arranged into those shapes which we see in the heaven. Some of ours, too, wish to prove by qualities and courses that there are no waters above the starry heaven, while yet asserting that the star of Saturn is the coldest. So they are asked why it is cold, which ought to be the hotter the higher it is and the nearer the heaven. For when a round mass is turned about, its inner parts move more slowly and its outer parts more quickly, and therefore more hotly; so it ought to be hot rather than cold. So the nearness of the waters above the heavens makes it cold.
03_marg112: And the evening and morning were, etc. MYSTICALLY. The morning of the second day begins from Noe, as from boyhood, and stretches to Abraham through another ten generations. And it is well compared to the second day, on which the firmament was made amid the waters: like Noe’s ark amid the lower waters, on which it floated, and the upper, by which it was rained on. This age is not blotted out by a flood, because our boyhood is not blotted out of memory by forgetfulness: for we remember that we were boys; that we were infants we do not remember. Its evening is the confusion of tongues among those who were making the tower, and morning comes from Abraham. But neither did the second age beget the people of God, because neither is boyhood fit for begetting.
03_interl69: Augustine: the second distinction of the divine works
03_marg113: The second day: AUGUSTINE. And it is to be noted that on the first day, when the light was made, it was said only: “Be light made,” and this in the Word, “and light was made” in the work; and at once the created light clung to the uncreated light, as nearer to it and more capable than every creature. On the second day there is some delay and a multiplying of words: “Let there be … made,” and “God made,” and “it was so”; so that we may understand these natures to be prone to failing and less fit for obeying.
03_marg114: JEROME. It is to be noted too that the works of this second day, according to the Hebrews, are not called good, though they are good like the rest; which is done on account of the number two, the chief of otherness, which first departs from unity and is set as a figure of bigamy and of many blameworthy things. Whence the animals that go into the ark by twos are unclean; the odd number is clean.
03_marg115: Or they are not called good because in this work the separating of the water is not made perfect; which is done in the next, where he says, “Let the waters be gathered together,” as will be said there.
03_marg116: AUGUSTINE. It is often asked what shape the heaven has. But the Holy Spirit, though our authors knew it, would not teach through them anything except what profits salvation. It is also asked whether the heaven stands still or moves. If it moves, they say, how is it a firmament? If it stands still, how do the stars fixed in it go round? But it can be called a firmament not because it stands still but because of its firmness, or because it is the uncrossable bound of the waters. And if it stands still, nothing hinders the stars from moving and going round.
03_marg117: MORALLY. On the second day there was made as it were the firmament of discipline, which distinguishes between fleshly and spiritual things as between the lower and upper waters.
03_marg118: ISIDORE. On the second day he set the firmament, namely the holy Scriptures, in the Church, of which it is said: “The heaven shall be folded together as a book.” By this firmament he divides the upper waters, that is, the people of the angels, who have no need to hear the word of God in reading. But he set that firmament over the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, looking up at it, they may know how he distinguishes between fleshly and spiritual things, as between upper and lower waters.

03_interl71: let them withdraw to one part of the earth
03_interl72: the unbelievers, who are shaken by the storm of lusts and the temptations of the floods
03_interl73: those thirsting for the fountain of faith
03_marg119: God also said: Let … be gathered together, etc. AUGUSTINE. On this day it seems to have been done that only the two lower elements were set apart. Yet it can be understood of the forming of the air, which then first received the form known to us, when the water, which filled the space of air and earth, withdrew into one part of the earth. So on the second and third day the four elements seem to have been set apart into their own forms. And since by the numbering of the days things formed out of the unformed are numbered, and Moses had already spoken of the heaven made out of bodily matter, whose form is far different from earthly things, what remained to be formed from it in the lowest part he would not put in with unusual words, by saying “Be … made,” because it was to receive a form weaker and nearer to unformedness; so that by these words, “Let the waters be gathered together, and let the dry land appear,” we may understand that here two things received their own forms, known and touchable to us: namely the waters, movable, and the earth, immovable. Whence the water is gathered, the earth appears; for water is slippery and flowing, earth stable and fixed.
03_marg120: Let the waters … be gathered together. BEDE. The waters which had filled everything between heaven and earth are gathered into one place, so that the light, which in the past two days had lit up the waters with clear light, might shine more clearly in the pure air; and the earth, which lay hidden and was muddy with waters, might appear and become dry and fit for sprouting. If it is asked where the waters were gathered which had covered all parts of the earth up to the heaven: it could happen that the earth, sinking down, offered hollow parts in which to receive the flowing waters. It can also be believed that the first waters were thinner, covering the lands like a mist, but were thickened by being gathered.
03_interl74: what pleased him in the Word pleased him in the work
03_marg121: And God called the dry land, Earth. AUGUSTINE. Earlier, to distinguish it from the waters, he called the whole more solid part of the world earth, saying, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” After the world begins to be formed and the face of the earth appears as the waters withdraw, to distinguish it from the part still pressed by waters, the portion which could be dry received the name earth (terra), because it is trodden (teratur) by feet. “And the gathering together of the waters, he called Seas.” For among the Hebrews all gatherings of waters, whether salt or sweet, are so called. And because, through the continuity of all the waters on the earth, he said they were gathered into one place, he now calls them in the plural gatherings of waters, on account of their many-branched bays.
03_marg122: Bede: though it is plain that there are many seas, yet he says the waters were gathered into one place, because they are all joined to the great sea. If some lakes seem shut in on themselves, yet by hidden passages they flow back into the sea. The diggers of wells too prove this, because the whole earth is filled through invisible veins with waters whose source is from the sea.
03_marg123: And God saw. BEDE. The earth was not yet sprouting, nor had the water brought forth living creatures, and yet God is said to see that it was good that the dry land had appeared as the waters withdrew; because the judge of the whole, foreseeing the things that are to come, praises as already perfect things that are still at the first start of the work; because with him the perfection of things is not in the finishing of the work but in the predestining of his will.
03_interl75: that is, let it be able to sprout
03_interl79: so that from its own weakness it may have compassion on the needy
03_interl80: from which like things may be propagated
03_marg124: Let the earth bring forth, etc. AUGUSTINE. The restraint of the orderer is to be noticed: although the creation of plants and trees is distinct from the kind of lands and waters, so that they cannot be numbered among the elements, yet because they are bound to the earth, fixed by their roots, he wished them to belong to the same day.
03_marg125: Let the earth bring forth, etc. BEDE. It is plain in these words that the world was finished and adorned in springtime, in which green plants are wont to appear and trees laden with fruit. And at the same time it is to be noted that the first shoots of plants or kinds of trees did not come forth from seed but from the earth; because at the one command of the Creator the dry land appeared, decked with plants and clothed with woods, which brought forth from themselves fruits and seeds of their own kind. For it was fitting that the form of things should come forth first perfect at God’s command, as man, for whom all things were made, was fashioned at the age of youth.
03_marg126: Augustine: it is also asked about thorns and thistles and certain fruitless trees, why or when they were created, since God said: “Let the earth bring forth the green herb, and such as may seed,” etc. But by the name of fruit some usefulness is signified. And there are many usefulnesses, plain or hidden, of all the things the earth nourishes by their roots. And we can answer outright that the earth brought forth thorns and thistles for man’s labour after sin; not that they were born elsewhere before, and afterwards in the fields man tilled, but both before and after in the same places; before, however, not for man, but afterwards. Whence: “shall it bring forth to thee,” that is, so that they begin to be born to thee for labour, which before were born only as fodder for the other animals.
03_marg127: Such as may seed. BEDE. All things were created perfect: man too was perfect in age, and the trees with leaves and fruit. Whence it is said here, “the fruit tree.”
03_interl83: GREGORY: the fodder of the word, the works of mercy
03_interl84: from wheat, wheat; from pulse, pulse
03_marg128: And the earth brought forth, etc. GREGORY. What the history bears witness to was truly done in such a way as to signify something else to be done. For the earth is the Church, which refreshes us with the fodder of the word and guards us with the shade of her protection; she feeds by speaking, she shelters by helping; so that she brings forth not only the herb of refreshment but also the tree of protection.
03_marg129: And the tree, etc. GREGORY. The tree brings forth seed according to its kind when our mind gathers from consideration of itself what it should do to another, and gives birth to the shoot of right work. Hence a certain wise man says: “See thou never do to another what thou wouldst hate to have done to thee by another.” And elsewhere: “All things whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them.” As if: look on each other as of your own kind, and know from yourselves what you ought to show to others.
03_marg130: Seed. STRABO. RABANUS. Sementis (seed) of crops and trees; semen of men and animals; seminium or sementum, the beginning of any thing.
03_marg131: Morally: on the third day, on which man prepares his mind to bear the fruits of good works, the stain and the waves of fleshly temptations being set apart, he has as it were dry land, the temptations being set apart, so that he can say: “With the mind I serve the law of God,” etc.
03_marg132: And the evening and the morning were: ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. The morning of the third day begins from Abraham, and the third age follows, like youth; and it is well compared to the third day, on which the earth was separated from the waters. For from all the nations, whose error is unsteady and moved by the empty teachings of idols as by every wind (which is well signified by the name of sea), the people of God was separated through Abraham, as the earth when the dry land appeared, that is, thirsting for the rain of the divine commandments; which, by worshipping one God, as earth watered so as to bear fruit, received the holy Scriptures and prophecies. This age could now beget a people to God, because the third age too, that is, youth, can now have children. Whence it was said to Abraham: “I have made thee a father of many nations,” etc. This age stretches from Abraham to David through fourteen generations. Its evening is in the sins of the people by which they passed over the divine commandments, up to the wickedness of Saul.
03_marg133: Bede: on the third day he gathered the lower and salt waters, namely the unbelievers, tossing themselves on the waves of lusts and temptations, and separated from them the dry land, that is, the faithful, thirsting for the fountain of faith. And he held in the unbelievers, lest by the waves of their iniquity they trouble the dry land, that is, the soul thirsting for God; but that it may be allowed to bring forth the fruits of good works and to love its neighbour, so as to have in itself seed according to its likeness, namely so that from its own weakness it may have compassion on another in need, and may bring forth a strong fruit-bearing tree, that is, a kindness in rescuing the oppressed and giving him the shade of protection.
03_interl86: here the adornments of the upper world are set in order
03_interl88: because near it, not because fixed in it
03_interl91: of fair weather and of storm
03_interl94: when they have finished their course
03_interl95: because preachers live and pass away at their own times. The earth first sprouted, then the lights were made, because after good works comes the enlightening of light to contemplate the beauty of the truth above
03_marg134: Let there be lights made, etc. AUGUSTINE. Because two days were assigned to the visible world, namely to the highest and lowest parts of the world, the remaining three were allotted to the visible and moving parts of the world which are created within the world. And because the heaven, made first, was to be adorned first, on the fourth the stars are made, by which the lower part might be lit up, so that it might not be dark for those who would live there. Provision was also made for the weakness of men, so that, as the sun goes round, they might have the alternation of day and night for the alternation of waking and sleeping. And so that the night should not remain unlovely, but men on whom the need of working at night fell might be consoled by the moon and stars; and there are some animals that cannot bear the light. And what is said, “and let them be for signs,” etc., seems to be said as if times began on the fourth day, whereas the first three days were not without time. For if any bodily or spiritual movement went before the making of the lights, so that something passed from future expectation through the present into the past, it could not be without time. Therefore we ought to take the times made by the stars not as spaces of duration but as the alternation of the states of the heaven; because the days and years we commonly know are made only by the movements of the stars. Or perhaps it was called day with respect to the form of the thing made, and night with respect to its privation; so that the matter not yet formed by form, from which the other things were to be formed, was called night. Or rather, in the thing itself made and formed, its changeableness, that is, the possibility of failing, is called night. For things can be changed even if they are not changed. And let evening and morning be understood not through the passing and coming of time, but through the bound by which it is understood how far the measure of the nature goes and whence it begins. Certainly, when he says “let them be for signs and for seasons,” he does not mean signs which it is vanity to observe, but signs of usefulness, namely those which sailors observe, or any men, to foresee the qualities of the weather. For of the sun it is certain that it completes its circuit in three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter, which is the solar year. So the other planets complete their years, shorter and longer. And the sun too serves the distinction of times, because, rising from the spring equinoctial circle to the summer solstice, and passing from there to the autumn equinox, and from there coming to the winter solstice, and at last returning to the spring equinox, it marks out the four seasons of the year. The moon, coming forth full in the evening after the spring equinox, makes the paschal limit, a rule that flourishes to this day. Of which, when it is asked whether it was made full or new, it is to be answered that God made it perfect, of whatever day it was; because, as they say, it was not fitting for God to make anything imperfect on that day. Others say the moon ought to have been made new, not on its fourteenth day, because no one begins to count so. Yet if God is said to have made something imperfect, it is not blameworthy. For what was begun by him was perfected by him and not by another. It is also believed to have been made full because the Septuagint has the words thus: the moon made at the beginning of the night; which happens when it is full.
03_marg135: Let there be lights made, etc. BEDE. Namely by that division by which the sun lights the day and the moon the night. For this, when the stars were made, was added to increase the first light: that the night too might come forth bright, lit by the brightness of the moon or the stars, which until then had known only darkness. For even if the night seems dark because the air nearest the earth is darkened, yet the higher spaces of the air are always bright with the shining of the stars.
03_marg136: Augustine: it is often asked whether these lights are bodies only, or have spirits ruling them and are breathed into with life by them, as the flesh of animals is given life through their souls. But about so obscure a thing nothing is to be rashly believed.
03_marg137: And let them be for signs, etc. BEDE. Because before the stars were made the order of times was marked by no signs, whether the midday hour or any other. So the lights are for signs, etc., not that times or days or years began from their making, but because by their risings and passings the order of times, days and years is marked.
03_interl96: lest man be brought into a dark dwelling
03_marg138: To shine, etc. BEDE. The lights always shine in the firmament, but they light the earth at fitting times. For sometimes the cloudy air stands in the way of their rising; and the sun, with its greater light, hinders the moon and stars from lighting the earth. Whence it is also called sol (sun), because it alone (solus) shines on the earth by day, the moon and the other stars being dimmed.
03_marg139: God made two great lights. BEDE. We can take the great lights as great not so much by comparison with others as in themselves, as the heaven is called great and the sea great. For the sun is called great because it fills the round of the earth with its heat, as the moon with its light; which, in whatever part of the heaven they are, light the whole earth and are seen by all. It is a great proof of their greatness that their disc appears the same to all men. For if it seemed smaller to those far off and larger to those near, it would be a sign of smallness.
03_marg140: A greater light, etc. BEDE. Namely the sun, not only in the form of its body but in the greatness of its light, because it lights up the lesser light and the stars. It is greater also in heat, because it warms the world, whereas in the days that passed before its creation the world had had no heat. And that the moon is seen as of one and equal size with the sun, they say comes from this, that the sun moves much farther from the earth and higher than the moon, and therefore its size cannot be perceived by us. For all things placed farther off seem smaller.
03_marg141: And a lesser light, etc. Even if it happens that the moon and greater stars are sometimes seen by day, yet it is plain that they bring the comfort of light not to the day but to the night.
03_marg142: AUGUSTINE. For the moon is seen at the beginning of the night when it is full, otherwise not; and it begins to be seen by day before its fullness, and in the course of the night.
03_interl100: for the adorning of the night
03_marg143: To shine, etc. These things can be understood of the great lights and of the stars, so that what is said, “to rule the day,” belongs specially to the sun, and what is added, “and the night,” to the moon and stars. But what is added, “to divide the light and the darkness,” fits all equally, which carry light about wherever they go. Whence: where they are not, they leave all things dark. If it is asked what kind of daylight there could have been before the creation of the stars, we answer: such as we see when the sunrise is drawing near and the sun has not yet appeared; namely when the day shines, the rays of the stars being dimmed, but the sun has by no means risen and shone.
03_marg144: Mystically: on the fourth day the lights shone in the firmament of heaven, that is, the teachers of the law, clinging to holy Scripture and showing the light of wisdom to those below. The crowd of stars came forth too, that is, the great number of learned men and those skilled in the law, who, shining in the night of this life, divide the things of Scripture perceived by the senses and by the mind, as between the light of the perfect and the darkness of sinners, making signs of virtues and miracles. Who are “for seasons and years,” because they live and pass away at their own times; but “the word of the Lord endureth for ever.” And it is well that the earth first sprouted and afterwards the lights were made, because after good works comes the enlightening by which the beauty of the truth above is seen.
03_marg145: Morally: on the fourth day, on which in that firmament of discipline the mind works and distinguishes spiritual understandings, it sees what is the unchangeable truth, which shines like the sun in the soul; and how the soul becomes a sharer in it and gives order and beauty to the body, as the moon lighting the night; and how all the stars, that is, spiritual understandings, shine in the darkness of this life as in the night.
03_interl104: because the things that pleased him to be made, once made, pleased him to remain
03_marg146: And the evening and morning were, etc. BEDE. In this evening the people of God offered the lamb in Egypt, and the true Lamb began the sacraments of his body. In this morning the people of Israel shook off the yoke of slavery, and Christ, redeeming us with his blood, freed us from the slavery of the devil. And this day of the fullest moon came forth fourth in the creation of the world. But at the time of the Lord’s passion, by the grace of a higher sacrament, it fell on the fifth day of the week, so that the Lord, crucified on the sixth day of the week, might rest in the tomb on the sabbath and rise on the first day of the week; on which he might give us the hope and faith of rising again and entering everlasting light.
03_marg147: And the evening was, etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. The morning of the fourth day is the kingdom of David. This age is like youth, which reigns among all the ages and is the firm firmament of all ages. Whence it is compared to the fourth day, on which the stars were made in the firmament of heaven. For the brightness of the sun figures the excellence of the kingdom; the brightness of the moon shows the people obeying the king, as the Synagogue. And the stars are its princes, and all things founded in the stability of the kingdom as in a firmament.
03_interl106: because water is nearer to heaven than earth is, the water creatures are set in order first
03_interl107: they are called creeping things of the waters, because few creep on the earth; more walk with feet
03_interl109: those reborn through the sacrament of baptism
03_interl112: not as far as the firmament
03_marg148: God also said: let the waters bring forth the creeping creature. After the face of the heaven was adorned with its lights on the fourth day, on the fifth day the lower parts of the world, namely water and air, are adorned with their animals.
03_marg149: Augustine: “God also said: let the waters bring forth the creeping creature,” etc. In creating the dwellers of the lower part, which is often called wholly earth, it was fitting that animals should be brought forth from the waters first, afterwards from the earth; because water is so like the air that the air grows thick with its breathings-out, and makes the blast of the storm and the winds, and gathers the clouds, and holds up the flying birds. So the order is kept that the animals of the waters are mentioned before those of the earth. Nor is it to be thought that any element was passed over, though he seems silent about the air. But the air is understood, in Scripture’s manner, to belong to the heaven, if there are any most peaceful spaces in its higher parts; or to the earth, because of the troubled and misty place which grows thick with moist breathings-out; though it too is sometimes called by the name of heaven. Therefore it is not said “let the waters bring forth creeping things and the air flying things,” but both are told to have been brought forth from the waters. For whatever of the waters is either flowing in waves or thinned out as vapour is reckoned to the moist nature. Whence some distinguish the elements so as to say that the eyes belong to fire, the ears to air; they assign smell and taste to the moist nature; and touch fits the earth. Yet fire passes through all, so as to make movement in them. For the soul begins its movement in all the senses from the fineness of fire, but in all does not come to the same point. In sight, the heat being held back, it reaches as far as its light. In hearing, the heat of fire passes as far as the clearer air. In smell, it passes the pure air and comes to the moist breathing-out, from which this thicker breeze stands. In taste, it passes this too and comes to the heavier moisture. When it has passed through that and comes to the earthly weight, it works the last sense, touch. He was not ignorant of this order who, bringing in the making of the things within the world, told first of the lights of heaven, afterwards of the creatures of the waters, last of those of the earth; nor did he pass over the air, but he reckoned its most quiet part to heaven, its troubled part to water or earth. Whence the psalm too, calling all the higher things heaven, “Praise ye the Lord from the heavens,” takes in all the lower things under the name of earth: “Praise the Lord from the earth,” etc., where the stormy winds and all the deeps are named. And this fire which burns the one who touches it, which arises from earthly and moist movements in such a way that it is turned into another element; and through this, being unable to escape into the higher calm, it is driven by troubled movements in this thicker part, to temper its rigour, and for the uses and terrors of mortals. But in the highest part the air is said to be so thin that it is neither shaded by clouds nor troubled by wind, nor holds up birds, nor feeds men, if any should happen to climb there, with a thicker breath, as this air does. Yet it is air, and it is believed to have been turned into a moist nature at the time of the flood. I have read too in a certain canonical epistle that the airy heavens perished in the flood; which is not to be understood except as turned into the nature of waters by the quality of the thicker air.
03_marg150: Having life: AUGUSTINE. That is, which are among living souls; as it is said, “the base of men,” that is, those who are base among men. Which some think is said because of slowness of sense, or because fish have no memory; but it is most certain that they have memory.
03_marg151: Augustine: there is a question about the changing of the elements. Some say all can be changed into all; others that there is something proper to each which cannot be changed into the quality of another. It is said too that nothing is seen without fire nor touched without earth, and so all are in all, but each has taken its name from what it has most of. And so, by the lack of heat, when the body grows too cold the sense is dulled, because the movement which is in the body from heat grows sluggish; since fire affects air, air moisture, and moisture earthly things, the finer passing through the thicker. So the higher air, because it belongs to the heavenly part, or because it has no visible inhabitant, was neither passed over, the heaven having been named, nor counted in the creating of animals. But the lower air receives animals only from the waters. For what is moist holds up the birds, which rest on their feathers as they fly, as fish swimming on certain wings of their own. Whence the flying things are said to have been brought forth from the waters. For the nature of the waters has been allotted a twofold place: the lower in the slipping wave, the higher in the blowing breeze; that to the swimming, this to the flying. From this element two senses are given to the animals: smell, by vapours; taste, for testing liquids. That we feel waters and winds by touch comes from this, that solid earth is mixed with all the elements, but is felt more in these thicker ones.
03_marg152: Under the firmament, etc. Though an immense space lies between, yet the birds that fly above the earth fly under the starry heaven, as men who are on the earth are said to be under heaven. Another translation: “beside the firmament of heaven,” because the spaces of this air which holds up the birds are near the ether.
03_marg153: Augustine: it is to be noted that certain philosophers so distributed its own animals to each element as to call earthly not only those that creep or walk on the earth, but also the birds that rest on the earth; the animals of the air, demons; the heavenly, gods, of whom we call part lights and part angels. Yet they assign to the waters fish and the beasts of their kind, so that no element is empty of its animals.
03_marg154: The demons are called animals of the air because they thrive in the nature of airy bodies; nor are they dissolved by death, because in them the element more fit for acting than for suffering prevails. For for suffering there are moisture and earth; for acting, air and fire. And the angels who transgressed, with their prince, now the devil, then an archangel, if they were in the purer part of the air before their transgression (for some of ours do not think they were heavenly or above-heavenly angels), it is no wonder if after sin they were thrust down into this mist, where yet there is air (if at least before sin they did heavenly works). Nor is it a wonder if they were changed by punishment into an airy quality, so that they can suffer from fire, that is, the element of a higher nature. Yet they have been allowed to hold only the misty places of the air, which is as it were a prison to them until the time of judgment.
03_interl113: from the greatest to the least
03_interl114: because there are water creatures which go not by creeping but by swimming or walking on feet, and there are flying things which have feathers but wholly lack flight; lest any kind seem passed over, he takes in generally every kind of creeping, swimming and flying things, and those that cling fixed to rocks, like the many kinds of shellfish
03_marg155: And every living creature: as distinct from man, who was to be made to the image of God, and, if he kept the commandments, would remain in perpetual unchangeableness. But the other animals were so made that some give way to others as food, or fail by old age.
03_interl115: this belongs to both kinds made from the waters, both to fish and to birds
03_interl116: which live either from the waters or from the earth
03_marg156: Increase and multiply: this belongs to both kinds of creatures made from the waters, that is, fish and birds; because as all fish can live only in waters, so do very many birds, which, even if they sometimes rest on land and produce their young, yet live not from the land but from the sea, and use the sea more gladly than the land. And what he adds, “and let the birds be multiplied upon the earth,” looks to both kinds of birds, namely those that live from the waters or from the land; because even the birds that do not live without waters, which often lie hidden in the depths like fish, are sometimes wont to come out upon the land, above all when they produce and rear their young.
03_marg157: Mystically: on the fifth day there were made in the waters the creeping things having life, that is, men renewed into life through the sacrament of baptism; there were made the flying things, that is, souls flying to things above.
03_marg158: Morally: on the fifth day the advanced mind begins to work in the actions of the troubled world as in the waters of the sea, for the profit of brotherly fellowship; and to bring forth, from bodily knowledges which belong to the sea, that is, to this life, creeping things having life, that is, works which profit living souls; and great whales, that is, the strongest knowledges, by which the waves of the world are broken and despised; and the fowls of the air, that is, voices preaching heavenly things.
03_marg159: And the evening and morning were: ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. The morning is the carrying away to Babylon, when in that captivity the people were settled lightly in leisure in a foreign land; and this age stretches to the coming of Christ, that is, the fifth decline, namely from youth to old age: not yet old age, nor any longer youth, but the age of the elder, which the Greeks call presbytes. For with them an old man is called not presbytes but geron. And indeed this age was so bent down and broken from the strength of the kingdom in the people of the Jews, as a man becomes older from youth. Which is well compared to the fifth day, on which animals were made in the waters and fowls of the air, after they began to live among the nations as in the sea, having an uncertain and unstable seat, like flying birds. There were the whales, that is, great men, who could rather master the waves of the world than serve in captivity; for they were perverted to idolatry by no terror. Where it is to be noticed that God blessed the animals, saying, “Increase and multiply,” because the nation of the Jews, scattered among the nations, was greatly multiplied. The evening, as it were, of this day, that is, of this age, is the multiplying of sins in the people of the Jews, because they were so blinded that they could not even know Christ.
03_interl118: the adornments of the lowest part
03_interl119: the flesh abstaining from evil works
03_interl121: Augustine: by imitating the life of the saints, as of neighbours
03_interl123: searching earthly things, through which they may understand heavenly ones
03_interl124: which harm with claw or tooth
03_marg160: Let the earth bring forth, etc. After the heaven was filled with stars and the air with flying things (it is called heaven because of its nearness), after the waters, which are near the air, were filled with their animals, it followed that the earth should be filled with its animals. For it has kinship with the waters, without whose moisture and watering it can neither bear fruit nor stand. So God commands the earth to bring forth cattle and creeping things and beasts of the earth. Under beasts is included whatever rages with mouth or claws, except serpents. Under creeping things, also serpents. By the name of cattle the animals that are in men’s use are designated. The rest of the four-footed beasts, such as deer and the like, we number among the beasts because of their untamed wildness. According to the old translation, in which it is written “four-footed beasts and creeping things and beasts of the earth,” by the name of four-footed beasts all are included except beasts and creeping things, whether tame or wild and of the field.
03_marg161: Let the earth bring forth. AUGUSTINE. HISTORICALLY. It followed that he should now adorn the earth with its animals. By saying “in its kind” three times, he signifies three kinds. First, in its kind, four-footed beasts and creeping things; where it can be understood which four-footed beasts he meant, namely those that are of the kind of creeping things, like lizards and the like. Whence in the repetition he did not repeat the name of four-footed beasts, because he understood them under the word creeping things. Therefore he did not say simply “creeping things,” but “every thing that creepeth on the earth”: for there are creeping things of the waters too. Therefore “every,” so as to include those that walk on four feet. By the beasts, of which he likewise said “in its kind,” he understood whatever rages with mouth or claws, except serpents. And the cattle, of which he said “in its kind” the third time, those that harm with neither, or with horns. How widely the name four-footed reaches can easily be known by the number of feet. And under the name of cattle and beasts every irrational animal is wont to be included.
03_marg162: In its kind: AUGUSTINE. These perhaps are said to be according to kind because they arose so that others are born from them and keep the form of their origin by succession. But this is not said of man, because one was made, from whom the woman too was made. For many kinds of men were not made, as of plants and trees, so that it should be said “according to its kind,” as if it were said “by kinds,” so that things alike among themselves and belonging to one origin of seed might be distinguished from the rest.
03_marg163: Augustine: there is a question about certain tiny animals: whether they were created in the first makings or from things produced. For very many are born from the corruptions of moist bodies, or from breathings-out, or from carcasses; some too from the rotting of trees and plants and fruits; and God is the author of all. But it can be said that the tiniest ones born from the waters and the earth were created then; among which those too are understood which are born from the things that arose when the earth sprouted. But as for those born from the bodies of animals, above all dead ones, it is absurd to say they were created along with the animals, except that they were sown beforehand in them in potency and in matter.
03_marg164: It is asked about poisonous and harmful creatures whether they were created after man’s sin for punishment, or rather were created harmless and began to harm sinners. So they could have been created to harm nothing, had there not been the cause either of frightening and punishing vices or of proving and perfecting virtue; because examples of virtue and patience are to be given to others, and man, being tempted, comes to know himself more surely; and rightly that health which was shamefully lost through pleasure is to be bravely recovered through pain. Yet beasts harm beasts that have no sin, so that it cannot be called punishment, nor do they receive virtue by such exercise. But some are the food of others; nor therefore would those on which others feed not rightly exist. For all things, as long as they are, have their measures, numbers and orders, all of which, rightly considered, are praised.
03_marg165: This too troubles: if harmful animals hurt the living as a penalty, train them for their health, or teach them unknowingly, why do they tear the dead for food? As if it mattered at all how the flesh, now lifeless, passes away, which is to be re-formed by wonderful power. Though from this too it is taught that no kind of death is to be dreaded for the sake of empty cares about our lifeless bodies.
03_marg166: So, though from this too a certain warning is given to the prudent, that they should so commend themselves to the Creator, who governs all things greatest and least by his hidden nod, by whom even our hairs are numbered, that they may not dread any kind of death for the sake of empty cares about their lifeless bodies, but may not hesitate to prepare the measures of holy courage for all things.
03_marg167: It is asked why there is not added here what was said of the animals of the waters: “And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply,” etc. Perhaps what had been said of the first creation of the living creature he left to be understood of the second, above all because he was going to say many other things in the works of this day. And the plants and trees, because they have no desire of begetting, he perhaps judged unworthy of this blessing. It was necessarily repeated in the case of man, lest anyone think there is sin in the office of begetting children, as there is in fornication without marriage.
03_marg168: Beasts of the earth, etc. BEDE. A change of order: it is of no concern in our speech what we name first in the order of creatures, since God created all things together.
03_marg169: Mystically: BEDE. ISIDORE. On the sixth day the earth brings forth the living creature when our flesh, abstaining from dead works, gives birth to living shoots of virtues according to its kind, that is, by imitating the life of the saints. Whence: “Be ye followers of me,” etc. We live according to our kind when we imitate the saints as neighbours. The earth brings forth beasts, that is, men proud in fierceness; and cattle, that is, those who live simply; and serpents, namely the crafty, and those who distinguish good from evil and, as if by creeping, search earthly things through which they may understand heavenly ones.
03_interl126: Bede: lest man enter an empty house
03_interl128: Bede: the things which serve men having been prepared
03_interl130: the worldly dwelling having been made and adorned, man was to be created as the dweller and lord of all
03_interl131: it suggests the unity of the Trinity
03_interl134: in holiness of ways and justification
03_interl137: over the irrational creature, lord of all lower things
03_marg170: Let us make man to, etc. AUGUSTINE. The plurality of persons is suggested, Father and Son and Holy Spirit; and at once the unity of the Godhead, when it is said, “And God made man to the image of God”: not the Father to the image of the Son only, for then it would not truly be said “to our image.” But it is so said, “God made man to the image of God,” as if it were said “to his own image.” And when it is said “to the image of God,” whereas above it was said “to our image,” it is signified that the plurality of persons does not bring about that we believe in several gods, but that we take Father and Son and Holy Spirit as one God.
03_marg171: Bede: “Let us make man to,” etc. It appears why it was said that the other things were made according to their kind and their species: for man was to be created, who should not only fit his kind and species but be made to the image of the Creator; the greatness of whose dignity is shown when, as if by a council of the persons, it is not said simply, as of the rest, “Let man be made,” but “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” In which the unity of the Trinity is shown and commended. For the Trinity is suggested in what goes before, when it is said, “God said: Let … be made,” and “God made,” and “God saw that it was good”; but more plainly when it is said, “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” For while there was no one to be taught, the preaching of the Godhead was hidden; when man began to be created, the faith and teaching of the truth shone out. For in saying “Let us make,” one working of the three persons is shown; and in “to our image and likeness,” one and equal substance of the Trinity. For it is not said by God to the angels, “Let us make man to our image and likeness”; for God and the angels do not have one and the same image or likeness. And man was created to the image of God not according to the body but according to the understanding of the mind; although in the body he has a certain property which shows this: that his stature is upright, by which the body fits the rational soul, because it is raised toward heaven.
03_marg172: It is asked how man was made immortal above the other living creatures, and received food in common with them. But the immortality of the flesh which we received in Adam is one thing; that which we hope for in the resurrection through Christ is another. He was made an immortal man in such a way that he could not die if he did not sin; but he would die if he sinned. But the sons of the resurrection, equal to the angels, will neither be able to sin nor to die any more. So our flesh after the resurrection will not need the refreshment of food, because neither by hunger nor weariness nor any other weakness will there be failing, nor can it be corrupted. Adam’s flesh before sin was created immortal in such a way that, helped by food, it would be free from death and pain, until, brought by bodily growth to the age that pleased the Creator, with offspring multiplied, he should at his command take also of the tree of life, by which, made perfectly immortal, he would no longer need the help of food. So the flesh of men was made immortal and incorruptible in such a way that they should keep their immortality and incorruption by keeping the commandments of God; among which was this too: that they should eat of the trees allowed, and abstain from the one forbidden; by eating these they would keep the gifts of immortality; by touching that, they would find death. But our flesh will be incorruptible and immortal at the end in such a way that, like the angels, it will always remain in the same state, and cannot need bodily food (which will not be there). For that the angels ate with the patriarchs was done not from need but from kindness, so that they might fit in more familiarly with men. Christ too ate after the resurrection, not that he needed food, but to show that after death he had taken back true flesh.
03_marg173: And let him have dominion: AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted also that when he had said “to our image,” he at once added: “and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea and the fowls of the air”; namely so that we may understand man to have been made to the image of God in that in which he surpasses the irrational creatures. And that is reason, or mind, or understanding, or whatever other name it may more fittingly be called, namely that in which he clings to contemplating the truth.
03_interl138: because everyone made spiritual and like God judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one
03_interl139: in reason, by which he clings to contemplating the truth
03_interl140: he repeats it to confirm it, and to impress more carefully what we were made
03_interl142: not the Father’s, not the Son’s
03_interl144: an anticipation: the woman was not yet formed
03_interl146: not together in time, but in foreknowledge
03_marg174: And God created man: he who works justice not by imitating some one of the saints but by gazing on the truth itself, so as to understand and follow the truth itself, receives here power over all things; because everyone made spiritual and like God judges all things, and he himself is judged by no one.
03_marg175: And he created, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that, as in the creating of the light it is said “Be light made,” and at once there follows “and light was made,” so when it is said “Let us make man,” there is brought in “And God made man to the image of God”; because this nature is intellectual, as that light is, and for it to be made is to know the Word through which it is made. For if it were said “and it was so done,” and there were added “and God made,” it would be understood as if made first in the knowledge of the rational creature and at last in a creature that was not rational. But how man was made immortal and received as food, with the other animals, the herb bearing seed, etc., is hard to say. For if he was made mortal by sin, before it he did not need these foods, because he could not be corrupted by hunger. For what is said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” though it seems it could not be done except through intercourse (whence here too there was a sign of mortal bodies), yet there could have been another way in immortal bodies: that children should be born from the affection of charity with no lust of corruption, neither succeeding parents who had died, nor themselves to die, until the earth should be filled with men; and so, a holy people having been established, such as we believe will be after the resurrection, even the manner of being born would be made. Some have supposed that the inner man was made now, and the body when he says “And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth”; they do not notice that male and female could have been made only according to the body. For lest it be thought that only the spirit was made, although only according to it was he made to the image of God, there is added, “male and female he created them,” so that the body may be understood to have been made. Again, lest both sexes be reckoned in one man, like those they call androgynes, he added in the plural “he made them,” although the woman was not yet divided from the man, but sown beforehand in matter.
03_marg176: Male and female, etc. AUGUSTINE. Afterwards it is set out more fully both whence and how men were made. But now they are briefly reported as created, so that the work of the sixth day and the dedication of the seventh may be set out with the rest. God created in the beginning one male and one female, not, as with the other living creatures, many in each kind, so that he might bind the human race with a firmer bond when it remembered that it had sprung from one. Whence, when he added, “male and female he created them,” he would not add “to the image of God,” which he left to be understood in the woman too by the unity of the joining. And they are well said to be created in this place, even if the manner of the creation is not set out, so that the divine blessing may fittingly be brought in, by which it is said: “Increase and multiply.” For the multiplying of men is brought about by the joining of male and female. So marriage is not to be condemned, which the blessing from above established for propagation, even if virginity is preferred.
03_marg177: Mystically: BEDE. ISIDORE. After these things God made man to his image and likeness, namely the perfect man who works justice by contemplating the truth itself; he receives power over the fishes of the sea and the fowls of the air, the cattle, the wild beasts and the creeping things, because, made spiritual and like God, he judges all things and he himself is judged by no one. “Male and female he created them,” because, as the woman to the man, so the less perfect ought to obey the spiritual and perfect man. For it is said to them, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” namely in spiritual gifts, so that reason may rule the flesh, as an unfeeling animal, and its disturbances. By the seed-bearing herb and the fruitful tree given to men for food we understand the offerings of the saints. Whence Paul: “If we have sown unto you spiritual things, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?”
03_interl147: the fruitfulness of the sex is received
03_interl148: by the steps of spiritual understanding
03_interl149: marriage fills the earth, virginity heaven
03_interl151: so that reason may rule every fleshly disturbance, as an unfeeling animal
03_marg178: What he had said of them before, as if taking counsel, he now says commanding: namely that they should have dominion over all creatures in the lower part of the world, which he goes through one by one.
03_marg179: BEDE. It is asked for what use man received dominion among the other living creatures, and for what uses or comforts these were created for man if he had not sinned. For not for food, but only herbs and the fruits of trees were granted at first. But perhaps, because God foreknew that man would sin and so become mortal whom he had created immortal, he established from the beginning those things by which, now mortal, he could protect himself, having from them food and clothing and help in labour. But after he would not be subject to his Maker, he rightly lost his dominion. Yet in witness of the first creation we read that birds served holy men, and the jaws of beasts and the venom of serpents gave way.
03_interl152: so that prelates may live from the offerings of those under them
03_marg180: BEDE. It is plain that before man’s sin the earth brought forth nothing harmful: no poisonous herb, no barren tree. For every herb and tree was given for food to men and to the fowls and to the living creatures of the earth. Whence it is plain that then animals did not live by eating animals, but fed together in harmony on herbs and fruits.
03_interl153: that is, man knew they were granted to him for food
03_marg181: AUGUSTINE. It is to be noted that where power is given to man to eat herbs and fruits, there is added “and it was so done,” in which it is signified that, at God’s saying this, man knew these were granted him for food, not that he ate at once. For if we refer what he says, “and it was so done,” to all the things said above, it will follow that we say they were already multiplied on the sixth day, which happened after many years.
03_interl154: he does not commend man specially as he does the rest, foreknowing that he would depart from order
03_marg182: And God saw all the things that he had made, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why, when the other things are each called good singly, man, made to the image of God, is called so only with the rest.
