But perhaps God foreknew that he would sin and not remain in the perfection of the image. For what is good singly is more so with all, but not the other way round. So care was taken to say what was true at present and would signify foreknowledge of the future. But God so ordered all things that, if some singly become deformed by sinning, yet the whole with them is always beautiful.
03_marg183: Mystically. ISIDORE. The morning of the sixth day is the preaching of the gospel through Christ. When the fifth is ended the sixth begins, in which the old age of the old man appears. For in this age that kingdom was violently worn down, when the temple was cast down and the sacrifices ceased; and now that nation, as to the strength of a kingdom, drags out as it were its last life. Yet in this age, as in the old age of the old man, the new man is born, who lives by the spirit otherwise. For on the sixth day it was said, “Let the earth bring forth the living creature,” etc., because on the fifth day it had been said, “Let the waters bring forth,” not the living soul but the creeping things of living souls. For as bodies are creeping things, so that people served bodily circumcision and sacrifices as in a sea of the nations. But he calls this a living soul because now eternal life begins to be desired. And the serpents and cattle which the earth brings forth signify the nations that would believe the gospel steadfastly, of whom it is said to Peter, “Kill and eat”; and when he called them unclean he heard, “That which God hath cleansed, do not thou call common.” Then man is made to the image and likeness of God, as in the sixth age Christ is born, of whom it is said, “And he is a man, and who shall know him?” And as on that day male and female, so in this age Christ and the Church. On that day man is set over the cattle and serpents and fowls of the air; and in this age Christ rules the souls obedient to him, which came partly from the Gentiles, partly from the Jews, that tamed by him they might grow gentle: those given to fleshly lust like cattle, or darkened by dark curiosity like serpents, or lifted up by pride like birds. On that day man and the animals that are with him are fed with seed-bearing herbs, fruit-bearing trees and green herbs. In this age too every spiritual man who is a good minister of Christ and imitates him as he can is fed spiritually with the people on the nourishment of Scripture and the divine law: partly for desiring fruitfulness of reasonings and words, as with seed-bearing herbs; partly for the profit of morals and human conduct, as with fruit-bearing trees; partly for the vigour of faith, hope and charity unto eternal life, as with green herbs, that is, thriving ones, which wither in no heat of tribulations. But the spiritual man is so fed that he understands many things; the carnal, that is, the little one in Christ, as God’s cattle, so that he believes even if he does not understand; yet all have the same foods. The evening of this age is that of which the Lord says, “Thinkest thou when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on earth?” After that evening there will be morning, when Christ will come in glory; then those will rest with Christ from all their works to whom it is said, “Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect.” For these do very good works, after which they will rest on the seventh day, which has no evening.
03_marg184: On the sixth day the earth brings forth the living soul, that is, man, from the stability of his mind, where he has spiritual fruits, that is, good thoughts, rules all the movements of his soul, so that there may be in him a living soul, that is, one serving reason and justice, not earthliness and sin. So man is made to the image and likeness of God, male and female, that is, understanding and action, by whose joining the spiritual offspring may fill the earth, that is, subdue the flesh, and the other things which have already been said of the perfection of man. In these, as in days, the evening is the very completion of each work, and the morning the beginning of the following.
03_interl156: causally indeed and in potency; whose numbers, growth and decline time would afterwards unfold visibly
03_interl157: by the perfection of the number six
03_interl158: the making of things was finished in six days; the repair of men is finished in six ages
03_marg185: ALCUIN. In no way can it be said how God made heaven and earth. But this account, by the order of the days, sets out as it were a history of things made, but above all keeps to a foretelling of things to come. If anyone is troubled that, in the ages of the world, the first two are unfolded in ten generations each, the three following in fourteen each, while the sixth is bounded by no number of generations, it is easy to see that in each man too infancy and childhood cling to the five senses of the body. But five doubled (because the human sex is twofold, whence such generations come about) makes ten. But from adolescence, where reason begins to prevail in man, knowledge and action, by which life is ruled and managed, are added to the five senses, so that it becomes seven; which, doubled because of the twofold sex, stands out in fourteen generations, which the three ages have, namely of the adolescent, the young man and the elder. But old age is ended by no fixed term of years; after those five ages, however long anyone has lived is reckoned to old age. In this age of the world too the generations do not appear, so that the last day too may be hidden, which the Lord showed it is profitable not to know.
03_marg186: So … were finished, etc. ALLEGORICALLY. After the very good works of those six days, as it were, let man hope for everlasting rest, and understand what it is that God rested on the seventh day from his works: because he himself works these good things in us, who commands us to work; and he is rightly said to rest because after all these works he will give us rest. As a householder builds a house, commanding his servants to do it, and afterwards, when the building is finished, is said to rest from his works because he bids them rest.
03_marg187: ISIDORE. MORALLY. Each of us has in our own works and right living, as it were, these six distinct days, after which he ought to hope for rest. On the first day, the light of faith, when he first believes visible things; for the sake of which faith the Lord deigned to appear visibly. On the second day there is made as it were the firmament between the lower and the higher waters. On the third day, on which he prepares and raises his mind to bring forth the fruits of good works, separated from the stain and the waves of fleshly temptations, he has his mind like dry land, that is, as if from the disturbances of the sea, so that he can now say: “With the mind I serve the law of God; but with the flesh, the law of sin.”
03_interl159: in himself, because afterwards he made nothing new
03_marg188: In the Hebrew it reads “on the seventh day.” So we shall press the Jews, who glory in the idleness of the sabbath, that already then, in the beginning, the sabbath was broken, when God worked on the sabbath, completing his works on it.
03_marg189: And … God ended, etc. AUGUSTINE. Another translation: “God finished on the sixth day the works which he made”; which raises no question, because the things made on it are plain. But according to the Hebrew truth it is to be asked how God is said to have completed his work on the seventh day, on which he is said to have created nothing new; unless perhaps he is said to have made that day itself then, and to have completed his work in making it, because when it was made he perfected the measure and number of the days, by whose cycle all ages roll on; for in the turning round the eighth is the same as the first. So he completed his work on the sixth day, the seventh being added, which he willed to be called and to be the sabbath, and gifted with a mystical blessing and sanctification above the rest. Whence the day of judgment too, because it will come after the seventh of the sabbath, is called the eighth in the Scriptures, as if only seven days had gone before; and the day of the Lord’s resurrection, though it would come after so many thousands of days, was called the eighth. It can be said that God completed his work on the seventh day because he blessed it and sanctified it; for blessing and sanctifying is a work; for Solomon did a work when he dedicated the temple.
03_marg190: And … God ended, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked whether those six days passed away and, the seventh being added, are now repeated through the rolling of the times not in reality but in name. For in all time many come that are like those past, but none the same. Whence it is doubted whether those six days have passed; or whether, while these usual days run past daily, those remain in the making of things, so that not only in the three before the lights but also in the remaining three we understand day in the form of the thing that was created, night in its failing or privation, namely when the form is lost by some change which is in every creature, either in possibility, when the effect is lacking, as in the heavenly bodies, or in act, as in earthly and mortal things; while evening in all is the end of the completed making, and morning the beginning of what is starting. For every creature is held within fixed beginnings and ends. But whether this or that or something else more likely be said, God perfected his works in the perfect number of days, that is, six; which he ordered in measure and number and weight, that is, in himself, who is measure, setting a limit to every thing, and giving numbers and form, and weight, because he draws all things to rest and stability; for he bounds, forms and orders all things. Or he so ordered all things that they should have measure, number and weight, as it is said, “God ordered bodies in colours,” not that the colours were in himself first, but that the bodies themselves should have colours. Nor is the number six perfect because God made his works in six days, but he perfected his works in six days because six is perfect. So it would be perfect without these; and unless it were perfect, the works would not have been made perfect according to it.
03_marg191: BEDE. Not as if weary from working, but he rested from all his work because he ceased to make a new creature. For to rest is used for to cease, as in the Apocalypse: “they rested not, saying: Holy, holy, holy,” that is, they did not cease saying it.
03_marg192: It is understood more deeply too that he rested from all his work, that is, that he had no need of those works in which to rest, whose rest in himself is true, always, without beginning and end; but that he made the works only for the sake of goodness, that they might rest in him. But human need labours daily that it may rest in its works, as God says, “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.” But God had no need to rest in his creatures, but gave rational creatures rest in himself.
03_marg193: And God rested, etc. God did not labour in working, who made all things by his word alone, saying “Be … made.” Nor does a man labour in saying “Be … made.” But perhaps he is said to have laboured in thinking what should be made, and to have rested from that care when the things were finished. But to think this is to be foolish. So for him to have rested is to have given the rational creature rest in himself, namely that we may be borne by desire to where we may rest, that is, seek nothing further. For as he is said to do what we do while he works in us, and to know when we know, so to rest when we rest by his gift.
03_marg194: AUGUSTINE. It is no wonder if, foretelling in this way the day on which Christ was to rest in the tomb, he said: “On the seventh day he rested,” afterwards to work the orders of the ages.
03_marg195: But it can be understood that God rested from making kinds of creatures, because he did not create new ones further; yet until now he works the governing of those same kinds which were then established. For the power of the Creator is the cause of every creature’s subsisting. For what is said, “My Father worketh until now,” shows the continual governing of the whole creation. On the seventh day he rested, so as to make no new creature further; but he works until now, so that he does not cease to hold together and govern what he made.
03_marg196: But God was neither wearied by creating nor refreshed by ceasing; but by his Scripture he urges us to the desire of rest, saying that he sanctified the day on which he rested; for he is not read to have sanctified the others, as if with him rest were of more worth than working.
03_marg197: It is a fault of the soul too to delight in its works in such a way as to rest in them rather than in itself away from them, since in the soul itself, or reason, there is something better by which it made them than the things it made. So God, when he is said to have rested, is shown to have delighted in no work as if he needed to make it, or would be less if he had not made it, or more blessed when he had made it. For what is from him owes him that it is; but he owes no one, because that he is blessed is from himself. By loving himself he set himself above the things he made. So he sanctified not the day on which he began to make them, nor that on which he made them, lest his joy seem to have grown by making them or having made them, but the one on which he rested from them in himself, who never lacked rest. But he showed it to us through the seventh day, signifying that it is given only to the perfect, to whom he assigned the day which followed the perfecting of all things. For he who is always at rest rested for us when he showed that he had rested, and rests in us when he grants us rest in himself. So the rest of God is that by which he needs no one’s good; and therefore it is sure for us in him, because we are made blessed by the good which he is, not he by the good which we are. Further, he who does not need the good he made needs no other good besides himself. For this is his rest from all the works he made: that he does not need the good he made, nor would need it if he had not made it. For thus he could be called needing no goods not by resting from things made but by making nothing. But if he could not make, there would be no power; if he could and did not, there would be great envy. But being almighty and good, he made all things very good. And because by himself, the good, he is perfectly blessed, he rested in himself from the good things he made, with that rest from which he never departed.
03_marg198: But if it were said that he rested from things to be made, it would be understood only that he did not make them; if from things made, he might seem to need the things made themselves. But let us rest not in ourselves but in him, and not wish to be so like God as to rest in ourselves as he does in himself. But as he rested only in himself, because he is blessed by himself, so let us hope to rest in him, since we are blessed not by our own good but by him.
03_marg199: God always rested in himself. But in the days in which the finishing of things is told, he rested only on the seventh, which follows the perfecting of things; for he rests from finished things who does not need finished things to be more blessed.
03_marg200: We see his works good; but his rest we shall see after our good works. To signify which he commanded one day of the sabbath to be kept; which in the time of grace is offered in this, that he keeps a perpetual sabbath who in hope of the future does all good things and does not glory in his good works as if he had not received them.
03_marg201: With him there is neither morning nor evening to his rest, because it is neither opened by a beginning nor closed by an end. But in finished works it has a morning and not an evening, because the finished creature begins to be turned to the rest of the Creator; but it has no end of its perfection. And so the rest of God begins not for God himself but for the perfection of things, and has a morning in that it is perfected by him; but in its own kind it is ended as it were by an evening, whereas in God it has no evening, because nothing will be more perfect than perfection itself.
03_marg202: In those days in which all things were being created, evening is the end of the creature made; morning the beginning of another to be made. And so the evening of the fifth day is the end of the creature made on it; the morning after it, the beginning of that to be made on the sixth day, whose evening is the end of what was made on it. And because nothing remained to be made, so after it morning came, not to be the beginning of another creature to be made, but of the rest of every creature in the Creator’s rest. For when the sixth day is completed, after its evening, a morning is understood, by which is signified the beginning of abiding and resting; which rest of God has neither beginning nor end; that of the creature has a beginning but not an end. For that is why the seventh day began from a morning but is ended by no evening. But if in the other days evening and morning signify changes of times such as pass daily, nothing forbids the seventh day too to be closed by evening and morning, so that the morning after the evening of the seventh day is the beginning of the eighth, of which nothing needed to be said, because it is the same as the first, to which it returns. Whence it is more likely that these seven days, following one another under the names of those, run through the times; but that those first ones, unfolded in a form unknown to us in the very making of things, remain; which we are forced to admit of the three that are recorded as made before the lights.
03_marg203: It is asked how God is said to have rested in himself on the seventh day, when it is written, “and God rested on the seventh day,” as if not in himself. What then is the seventh day? A creature, or a span of time, which too was created together with the temporal creature, and so a creature? For there are no times which were not created by God. But the six days, with and in which the creatures were created, have been spoken of above. But when did he create the seventh? For on it he made nothing, but rested from the things he had made. How then did he rest on a day which he did not create? Or how did he create it after the six days, since he finished all things on the sixth day and created nothing on the seventh? Perhaps God created only one day, so that by its repetition many would pass; nor was there need for him to create seven, because the seventh repetition of the one he had created made this one. For he divided the light from the darkness and called it day, and the darkness night. The repetition of this day Scripture calls the second day, then the third, and so on up to the sixth, on which he finished his works; whose repetition received or took the name of the seventh day. And so the seventh day is no day and no creature except that which was made before and called day.
03_marg204: But how could the light go round to show the change of day and night, not only before the lights but before the firmament was made, indeed before the form of earth or sea that would allow the light to go round? Driven by this difficulty we said above that the light was made first as the finishing or strengthening of the spiritual creature; but night, the matter still to be formed in the other works, which had been established when God first made heaven and earth and all the rest.
03_marg205: But it is easier for us to admit that we do not know how the light called day, if it is bodily, brought about the change of day and night by its going round; or, if it is spiritual, whether it was present to all things to be made, and by its presence made day, by its absence night, evening by the beginning of its absence, morning by the beginning of its presence; than that we should try, against the nature of divine Scripture, to say that the seventh day is another day than the seventh repetition of that day which God made. Otherwise either God did not create the seventh day, or it is seventh after those six, and it will be false that he finished all his works on the sixth day.
03_marg206: But since we do not find by what going round bodily light, before the heaven was made, showed night and day, we end the question thus. The light first created was not bodily but spiritual; as it was made after darkness, that is, turned from its formlessness to the Creator, so after evening it has morning, when after the knowledge of its own nature, by which it is not what God is, it turns itself back to praise the light which is God, by whose sight it is formed. And because the lower creatures are not made without its knowledge, one day is repeated everywhere, by whose repetition as many days are made as the kinds of things are distinguished, to be ended in the perfection of six; so that the evening of the first day is its knowledge of itself, by which it knows it is not what God is; the morning after the evening, by which one day is closed and the second begun, is its turning, so that it refers what it is as created to the praise of the Creator, and receives from the Word of God the knowledge of the creature which is made after it, that is, the firmament; which is made first in its knowledge, when it is said, “and it was so done,” and afterwards in the nature of the firmament, when there is added, “and God made the firmament.” Then the evening of this light, when the firmament is known not in the Word of God, as before, but in its own nature; which knowledge, as being lesser, is called evening. Afterwards morning comes, by which the second day is closed and the third begins; in which likewise the morning is the turning of this light to the praise of God, because he made the firmament, to receive from the Word of God the knowledge of the creature to be made after the firmament. And so the rest, up to the morning after the evening of the sixth day. For there is much difference between the knowledge of each thing in the Word and in its own nature. Whence the one belongs to the day, the other to the evening. For the knowledge that is seen in the Word shines out, and that by which the creature is known in itself is rightly called evening.
03_marg207: And because the angels so know the creature in itself as to put before it that they know it in the Truth through which all things were made, through the six days night is not named, but after evening and morning, one day, and so through the rest. So by the sixfold repetition of the day, whose evening and morning can be taken by the reasoning given above, every creature was made; and the morning came by which the sixth day should end and the seventh begin, without evening, because the rest of God is not a creature, which through the other days is known as made in one way in God and in another in itself; the as it were faded form of which knowledge makes the evening. So day is not to be understood as the form of the work, evening as its end and morning as the beginning of another work, lest we be forced to say that a creature of the seventh day was made besides the six days, or that the day itself is not a creature; but the same day is repeated through all the works, not by a bodily going round but by spiritual knowledge, when the angels first contemplate the creature in the Word of God, then in their own knowledge, and afterwards in itself, which is signified by the evening coming; and they refer this knowledge to the praise of the Truth itself, which the morning signifies.
03_marg208: It is understood also that the rest of God on the seventh day, not for the creature but for himself, had a morning without evening, that is, a beginning without end. For if it were said “he rested on the seventh day,” and “from his works” were not added, we would seek in vain the beginning of the rest; for he does not begin to rest. But the rest from works began from the time he finished them. For he would not have rested from his works by not needing them before they existed, which he did not need even when finished; and because he never needed them at all, neither is the blessedness by which he does not need them perfected as if it were to be perfected. Therefore no evening came to the seventh day.
03_marg209: Nor let anyone think that what has been said of the spiritual light, and of the spiritual day made in the spiritual and angelic creature, of the contemplation which it has in the Word of God, and of the knowledge by which the creature is known in itself and its being referred to the praise of the Truth, fits the understanding of day, evening and morning not properly but figuratively and allegorically. It fits otherwise than in the custom of this bodily light, yet not as if properly here and figuratively there. For where the light is surer, there the day is truer; why then not a truer evening and a truer morning?
03_marg210: So that first day, namely the angelic creature, was presented to all the works of God by this order of presence, the order of the knowledge by which it foreknew in the Word the things to be made and knew in the creature the things made; not by intervals of times, but having a before and after in the connection of the creatures, it knew all things together in the working of the Creator. For God made future things so that he did not make temporal things in time, but they, made by him, should run through the times. For the light, the spiritual creature, could be presented to all the works of God through the perfection of six, and from there have the morning of the rest of the seventh day, not an evening; so that God’s having rested on the seventh day is not as if he needed it for rest, but that in the sight of the angels he rested from all his works only in himself, who was not made; that is, so that the angelic creature, which was presented as a day with an evening for knowing the works in him and in themselves, should know nothing better after all the very good things than him who rested from all his works in himself, needing none of them to be more blessed. In which knowledge, having no evening, it deserved for this to be blessed and sanctified.
03_marg211: ALLEGORICALLY. Whence it is said, “Remember that thou keep holy the sabbath day.” But this blessing and sanctifying signifies a greater blessing and sanctifying. For as by frequent victims the blood of Christ, to be shed once, was signified, so by the rest of the seventh day, often kept after the works of six days, was signified that sabbath day on which Christ was once to rest in the tomb, having finished on the sixth day all the works by which he restored the world, which was finished in six days; on which, mindful of the old work, he declared that he had finished the salvation of the world. For he said, “It is consummated,” and bowing his head he gave up the ghost. This sanctifying and blessing and rest after very good works signifies that we, after good works (which he himself works in us), shall come to the rest of the heavenly life, to enjoy eternal sanctification and blessing. Therefore this day is not written to have an evening.
03_interl163: the conclusion of what went before
03_interl166: Augustine: the matter of all visible things
03_marg212: BEDE. He touches those who say the world has always been, without beginning; or who think it was made by God, but from matter which he did not make but which is co-eternal with him. “In the day that he made heaven and earth,” etc. He puts day for the whole time in which the first creation was formed; for heaven was not made or lit with stars, and the earth separated from the waters and planted with trees and herbs, on any one of the six days. So the Apostle, saying, “Behold, now is the day of salvation,” signifies the whole time in which we live here. But it is hard to understand how God made heaven and earth and every plant on this day, unless we say that in formless matter every creature was formed alike, according to that saying: “He that liveth for ever created all things together.” If then by this day we understand the time in which all things were made together before every day of this world, it is plain that the herb and every tree were made causally in one substance before they visibly rose and sprouted. But if we take this day for that time in which the world was adorned through six days, we can understand that the earth brought forth the green herb not as now, when many things are produced by the watering of rains or the industry of men, but the first creation of herbs and trees was made otherwise, namely by God’s command alone, without rain and human work. Whence there follows: “for the Lord God had not rained upon the earth.”
03_marg213: ISIDORE. “These are the generations of the heaven and the earth.” The six days have been counted, in which the whole of the world from head to end is figured as in a brief image. Whence this part of the book is called the book of the generation of heaven and earth. But in this conclusion one day is spoken of, on which God made heaven and earth, etc., in which time is signified. In these few words, then, the whole creation before the sin of the soul is suggested: in heaven and earth, every visible creature; by the name of day, all time, because time and temporal things were made together; by the name of plant and herb, the invisible creature, because of the unfading vigour of life if it had not sinned. “Before it sprung up in the earth,” that is, before it sinned, that is, subjected itself to earthly desires. Whence there follows: “for God had not rained upon the earth,” that is, he had not yet made the soul live by sending the rain of the word from the clouds of prophets or of the gospel. “And there was not a man to till the earth,” because after sin man began to labour on the earth and needed those clouds, from which the plant, that is, the soul, grew green. The fountain of life watered it, that is, the flood of truth speaking in its understanding, so that it did not need rain from the clouds before it sinned. This was the state of man before sin.
03_marg214: Another translation has here: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth. When the day was made, God made heaven and earth and every green thing of the field,” etc. The view is made firmer by which it is said that God made one day, whence those six or seven days could be numbered by the repetition of this one, when Scripture, concluding all that it had said from the beginning up to here, says: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made.” For heaven and earth are not recalled as in the beginning, before the day was made, when darkness was upon the deep, but how heaven and earth were made when the day was made, the kinds of things being now distinguished, of which every creature is composed into this form which is called the world. Here then is recalled the heaven, which is the firmament, with all that are in it, and that earth which holds one place with the deep, with all that are in it. For when it is said, “when the day was made,” whether it is joined to what goes before, so that it is one sentence, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth, when the day was made,” or to what follows, so that the sentence is full, “When the day was made, God made heaven and earth,” it forces heaven and earth to be understood in this way, namely as they were made when the day was made. And when there is added, “and every green thing of the field,” which was made on the third day, it plainly appears that that is the one day which God made, by whose repetition the second and third day were made, and the rest up to the seventh. For since he wanted every creature to be taken under the name of heaven and earth, he added “every green thing of the field,” to signify this day more openly. For when we recall the order of the things made, we find the green thing of the field created on the third day, before the daily day was run by the presence of the sun. When too we hear, “when the day was made, God made every green thing of the field,” we are reminded of that day, which we understand either as a bodily light unknown to us or as a spiritual one in the fellowship of the angels. Again, when God is said to have made heaven and earth, etc., when the day was made, it is signified that he made all things together; and when the things created are recalled in the order of six days and are now brought back to one, we understand this one repeated seven times, and that sixfold or sevenfold repetition not made by an interval of time. For Scripture mocks the proud by its height, holds the attentive by its depth, feeds the great with truth and the little ones with kindness.
03_marg215: In the first making of the world, when God created all things together, man was made as the reason for creating man, not the act of man created. But these things are in one way in the Word of God, where they were not made but are eternal; in another way in the elements of the world, where all things to come were made together; in another way in things which are created now not together but each in its own time; in another way in seeds, in which again the first causes are repeated, drawn from things which came to be according to the causes which he first made, as the herb from the earth, the seed from the herb.
03_interl167: of all invisible things, because of the vigour of life
03_interl169: every green thing of the field, which appears to have been made on the third day
03_interl171: evil desire grew together in the mind
03_interl172: as if the shrubs or herbs were not born by the coming of rains; nor is it read to have rained until the flood
03_interl173: by the preaching of the prophets or of the gospel
03_interl175: there was no need for the hearts of men to be watered by human work
03_marg216: Every plant, etc. AUGUSTINE. The earth is understood to have brought forth the herb and the tree causally, that is, to have received the power of bringing them forth. For in it, as in roots, were made the things which would be through the times. So he made them before they were upon the earth, according to the formableness of the matter, the things to be formed by his word, the matter going before the forming not in time but in origin.
03_marg217: For … had not rained, etc. AUGUSTINE. As if God did not make them then as now, when it rains and men work, and through delays of times things come to be which were not, when he made all things together. For times did not exist before the creature, but with the creature, and are themselves a creature. For if there were no movement of the bodily or spiritual creature, by which future things succeed past ones through the present, there would be no time at all, nor could the creature be moved.
03_interl176: of wisdom, divided into four parts of virtues
03_interl179: breathing into hearts things useful and honest
03_marg218: But a spring, etc. BEDE. Whatever the watering of this spring was, it came upon the earth already clothed with herbs and trees. One spring is said to have risen, for some unity in the hollows of the earth; or the singular is put for the plural.
03_marg219: But a spring, etc. AUGUSTINE. Here he seems to make known the things that come about through intervals of times from the first making, where all things are made together, beginning from the element from which all the shoots of animals, herbs or trees are born, so that they may run the temporal numbers allotted to their own natures. For the first beginnings of all seeds are moist and grow from the moist. If it is said that no spring however great could water the whole face of the earth, and that if it watered the mountains it would be a flood, the answer is that it could be done by turns, as the Nile waters the plains of Egypt. By the one spring many springs can also be understood, watering their own regions; and the whole face of the earth watered, as the whole face of a garment is said to be coloured though not continuously but in spots. The things told from this spring come about through delays of times, not together. Since, then, the reasons of creatures are in one way in the Word of God, in another way the works from which he rested on the seventh day, in another way those which he works from them until now, the last we know somehow by bodily sense and custom; the two removed from our senses and from the use of human knowledge are first to be believed on divine authority, afterwards to be known somehow through those that are known.
03_interl182: that is, he gave the spirit of the power of contemplation
03_interl183: he quickened him with rational life
03_interl184: He quickened the whole body indeed, but this part is adorned with the senses for gazing on higher things, by which the rational soul is naturally clothed so as to savour the things that are above.
03_marg220: Formed, etc. AUGUSTINE. MYSTICALLY. A fuller account of man is unfolded figuratively, to instruct and exercise those who seek. This forming is not the beginning of a new work but a careful going over it again. If here we understand man as already made of body and soul, this mixing is well called slime. For as slime is made by mixing dust and liquid, so the soul, by quickening the matter of the body, unites it and does not let it be dissolved. “He breathed into his face the breath of life”: if there was only a body, we here understand the soul joined to the body. But if the man made was already body and soul, by this breathing sense was added to the soul when man became a living soul; not that that breathing was turned into a living soul, but it worked a living soul. Yet we ought not yet to understand a spiritual man, but a natural one, who was made spiritual when he was set in the blessed life of paradise. Whence we are first natural, born from him after sin, until through the spiritual Adam we are reborn spiritual. By the name of paradise the blessedness in which man was placed is signified. But because men’s delightful rest is in groves, and to the senses of the body light rises from the east and the heaven rises up, which is higher and more excellent than our body, by these words the spiritual delights which the blessed life has are set out. We understand every tree fair to the sight of the understanding and good for food that is not corrupted to signify our spiritual joys, as is every spiritual reason and virtue, which is the food of the soul. This tree was brought forth from the earth because spiritual joy ought to be above the earth. The tree of life planted in the midst of paradise, because the soul ought to understand that it is set in the middle of things, so that while it has the bodily creature beneath it, yet it understands the nature of God to be above it, so that it neither despises what it is nor claims what it is not.
03_marg221: “And the Lord God formed man,” etc. First a natural body, such as we now have, was formed from the slime of the earth, not a spiritual one, such as we shall rise with. Whence it is asked how we are re-formed, if we are not re-formed through Christ to what we were in Adam; but he did not lose immortality if he was natural before; nor will the body be natural but spiritual when it has put on incorruption. Whence some have thought that man was natural in body but was changed when he was placed in paradise, as he will be changed in the resurrection. But if this is so, we try in vain to take paradise and those trees and the fruit according to the proper sense of things done. For food from the fruits of trees is not needed by immortal bodies. The very death of man, too, which he deserved by sin, shows that he would not have died if he had not sinned. But how is he mortal without death? Or how, if the body was natural, was it not mortal? Whence they think he deserved by sin not the death of the body but of the soul, believing that because of the natural body he would have gone out of this body to the rest which the saints now have, and at the end of the world received the same body immortal. Against which is the Apostle: “The body indeed is dead because of sin.” And so he would not have died even in the body if he had not sinned; yet he could be natural before sin, and after a life of justice in paradise be made spiritual when God willed. But they say: How are we renewed if we do not receive back what the first man lost? We do receive it in a way, and we receive it. For we do not receive back the immortality of the spiritual body, which man did not yet have, but the justice from which man fell by sin. We shall be renewed from the oldness of sin, not into the natural body in which he was, but into a better, that is, a spiritual one. We are renewed in mind according to the image of God, which was lost by sinning; we shall be renewed in flesh when this corruptible and mortal shall put on incorruption and immortality, into which Adam was to be changed, had he not deserved by sinning the death of the natural body. The Apostle does not say the body is mortal because of sin, but dead. For before sin it was mortal and immortal, because it could die and not die. But it is one thing not to be able to die, another to be able not to die. In one way man was created immortal, which he had from the tree of life, not from the condition of his nature. He was mortal by the condition of a natural body, immortal by the gift of his Maker. For nothing will be immortal in such a way that it cannot die at all except the spiritual. So through sin what was mortal was made not mortal but dead, which it would not have become had he not sinned. For this body is natural, like the first man’s; but now it is worse, for it has the necessity of dying.
03_marg222: The first robe is either the justice from which he fell, or, if it signifies bodily immortality, he lost this when by sinning he could not come to it. So Adam had a natural body not only before paradise but also in paradise, although in the inner man he was spiritual; which he lost by sinning, and deserved the death of the body, who by not sinning would have deserved a change into a spiritual body.
03_marg223: Formed, etc. We must see whether this is a summing-up, so that it is said how man was made, whom we read was made on the sixth day; or whether, then, when he made all things together, he made man too among them, so that with the passing of time he should also be made in this way, by which he leads his life in this visible form; as the grass was made before it sprang up, and with the passing of time and the watering of the spring it sprang up so as to be upon the earth.
03_marg224: Let us look first at the summing-up. Perhaps man was made on the sixth day, as the day itself was made first, as were the firmament, the earth and the sea; which are not to be said to have been made before in the first beginnings and to have lain hidden, and afterwards, as the times passed, to have shone forth as if sprung up into this form with which the world is furnished. Nor were the stars first made in the elements and hidden away, to flash out into these forms as the times passed; but all things were created together in the perfection of six when the day was made. So perhaps on the sixth day man was made of slime in this visible form, but then it was not recalled which is now suggested by summing up. But this does not seem to fit Scripture. For it is written, while the works of the sixth day were still being told, “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” So man had already been made of slime, and the woman from his side; for the male was not made on the sixth day and afterwards, as time passed, the female. For he says: “male and female he created them.” How then was the woman made when the man was already placed in paradise, as follows? But perhaps Scripture recalls what was passed over. For by this, paradise was planted on the sixth day, where the man was placed and put to sleep so that Eve might be formed; and when she was formed he awoke and gave her a name. But the words of the man, either when he gave names to the animals or to the woman, or when he said, “Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother,” could only have come about with a delay of time. So these things were not done as all things were created together. Either, then, not all the works of the six days were made together but through delays of times; or, if they were made together, according to that saying, “He that liveth for ever created all things together,” there is no doubt that man’s being formed from the slime of the earth, and his wife’s being formed for him from his side, belong not to the making in which all things were made together but to that which comes about through the times, by which God works until now. Which is hinted by these words: “God planted paradise in Eden, and brought forth still from the earth every tree,” etc. For when he says “still,” he shows that he brings forth in one way now, in another way then, when perhaps on the third day the earth brought forth the green herb, etc.; then, namely, in potency and causally, as all things are created together; now visibly, with the passing of time. Unless it be said that not every kind of tree was made on the third day, but some was put off, to be formed on the sixth day when man was made and placed in paradise. But all the works were divided by single days in vain if any mixing remained. So male and female were created in one way on the sixth day, in another way now; not then and not afterwards, or afterwards and not then, nor others afterwards, but the same in one way then and in another way afterwards: namely visibly, yet not from parents, but he from slime, she from a rib; but then invisibly, in potency and causally, as things to come are made, not made things.
03_marg225: Formed, etc. The making of man, who was made on the sixth day, is described more fully: that he was made, namely, in body and soul, the body from slime, but the soul created from nothing by God’s breathing; and the woman from the side of the sleeping man. But let us not think in a fleshly way that God formed the body with bodily hands, or breathed the soul or life with a throat. For what is said, “Thy hands, O Lord, have made me and formed me,” is a figure of speech. For God is a spirit and not composed of the outlines of limbs. So he formed man from slime, that is, by his word he commanded him to be made from slime. “He breathed into his face the breath of life”: that is, he created the substance of the soul and spirit in which he should live.
03_marg226: It is asked whether God made man suddenly in the age of manhood, or by perfecting him and increasing his ages, as he now forms him in his mother’s womb. But whichever of these he did, he did what befitted God, almighty and wise. For he so distributed the laws of times to the kinds and qualities of things that his will is above all. For by his power he gave numbers to the creature; he did not bind that power to them; nor were days waited for so that Moses’ rod should be turned into a serpent. Nor are such things done against nature, except for us, to whom the course of nature is known otherwise; but for God, what he made is nature. So Adam was made at once in the age of manhood; whom yet he made according to the causal reason in which he was made before; otherwise he would not have made him in the works of the six days. Nor would he act against his own disposing; for in the first making of causes it was possible for man to be made thus, but it was not necessary there. For this was not in the making of the creature but in the good pleasure of the Creator, whose will is necessity. But we, in things arisen in time, know what the nature of each is, which we learn by experience; but whether it will come to be we do not know. It is in the nature of a young man to grow old; but whether it is in God’s will we do not know; for that will necessarily come to be which he wills and foreknows. Many things will come to be according to lower causes which will not come to be in the foreknowledge of God. But if they are otherwise there, they will rather come to be as they are there, where he foreknows who cannot be deceived. For old age is in the future of a young man; but it is not in the future if he is to die first. For according to certain lower causes of things to come Ezechias was to die, to whom God added fifteen years, which before all things he foreknew he would do. So he did not do what was not to come; for that was rather to come which he foreknew. So according to lower causes he had already ended his life; but according to the will and foreknowledge of God, who knew from eternity what he would do, he was to end it then when he ended it. For even if it was granted to him praying, he who foreknew also knew that by praying he would deserve it, and therefore it was necessarily to come.
03_marg227: And breathed, etc. AUGUSTINE. Without doubt it is to be said “blew” or “breathed,” not that he breathed with a throat or formed or created the soul of man from his own substance; but he blew, that is, he made a breath of man, namely the soul. For to blow is to make a breath; to make a breath is to make a soul. Whence: “I have made every breath.” But it is asked whether he made the soul from nothing, or from a thing which was already made but was not a soul. For if we say that God creates nothing from nothing after he created all things together, we do not believe he still creates souls from nothing. But if there was a matter from which the soul was made, or from which souls are still made, what is it? What name, what form, what use does it hold among things made? Does it live or not? If it lives, what does it do? What does it do or bring about in the whole? Does it lead a blessed life, or a wretched one, or neither? Does it quicken anything or not? If there was no life, how was it the incorporeal and lifeless matter of a future life? Either this is false or too well hidden. If it lived, neither blessedly nor wretchedly, how was it rational? If it was made rational when the nature of the human soul was made from that matter, an irrational life was the matter of the rational, that is, the human, soul. What then set it apart from the soul of a beast? It is to be said, then, that God in those first works, which he created all together, created the human soul too, which he would breathe into the body in its own time. For what is said, “to his own image,” is understood in the soul; “male and female,” in the body. Let it be believed, then, that man was so made on the sixth day that the causal reason of the human body was made in the elements of the world, but the soul itself was created, as the day was created first, until he should put it into the body formed in its own time. But if the soul was already made, where would it be better for it than there? Why then, living innocently, was it put into flesh, in which it would offend its Creator and deservedly perish? But perhaps it willed to be inclined to rule a body, where it could live justly and unjustly, and had what it chose: either reward for justice or punishment for injustice. Why then should it not be believed that it came to the body at God’s nod? Where, if it would obey, it would receive eternal life; punishment if it despised.
03_marg228: AUGUSTINE. It is to be said that the soul was not so created as to foreknow its future just or unjust work. For it is not believable that it would incline of its own accord to the life of the body if it knew it would so sin as to be punished with everlasting punishment. He who wills this creature to be so speaks against the goodness of God; but he who will not have it pay the penalty for its sins is an enemy of the truth.
03_marg229: Those are not to be heard who think the soul is a part of God. For if this were so, it could not be deceived either by itself or by another, nor be forced to do or suffer evil, nor be changed for better or worse. But the breath by which he quickened man was made by God, not of God. Nor is a man’s breath, which he makes, a part of himself, since he makes it not from himself but from the airy breath taken in and poured out. But God could make from nothing a living and rational thing, which man cannot. Some think, however, that man was not quickened when God breathed into his face and he became a living soul, but received the Holy Spirit. But it is not lawful to doubt that the soul was made from nothing.
03_marg230: It is often asked whether, if it does not wish to be embodied, it is forced. But it is better taught that it wills this naturally, that is, that it is so created as to will it, as it is natural for us to will to live. But to live badly belongs not to nature but to a perverse will. But if anyone will not think it was made except when it was breathed into the formed body, what will he answer when it is asked whence it was made? He will either say that God made something from nothing after that finishing of the works, or that it was made from something already existing, and he will labour in seeking what that nature is. But if he wants to avoid this by saying that man was made from the slime of the earth on the sixth day but recalled afterwards by summing up, let him see what he will say of the woman, since “male and female he made them.”
03_marg231: But perhaps the souls were made on the sixth day, where the image of God shines out, so that the bodies might be formed afterwards; but Scripture does not let us believe this, both because of the sixfold perfection of the works, and because the sexes, male and female, are only in the body. If anyone thinks both sexes are to be taken in one soul according to understanding and reason, what will he say of the things given for food at that time, which suit only bodies? But if he takes them figuratively, he will depart from the proper sense of the thing done, which is to be put first in such matters.
03_interl186: as if, where God placed him
03_interl189: a garden of delights; in Hebrew, Eden
03_interl191: Bede: the waters being removed from the surface of the earth
03_interl194: JEROME. It appears that he had made paradise before he made heaven and earth
03_interl195: it is given to be understood that man was not made there, because God foreknew that he would sin and be driven out from there to this earth, where he made him
03_marg232: And the Lord had planted, etc. BEDE. From that beginning he planted paradise, in which he commanded the whole earth, the waters being removed, to bring forth herbs and trees. In it he placed man, formed on the sixth day; and even if it holds a figure of the present Church or of the future homeland, yet according to the letter it is to be understood as a most delightful place, great with fruitful trees and fertile with a great spring. Where we say “from the beginning,” the old translation says “toward the east.” Whence they would have paradise to be in the eastern part, set apart by a long stretch of sea or land from the regions that men inhabit; whence not even the waters of the flood reached there. How it was planted he explains, saying: “And the Lord God brought forth of the ground every tree,” etc. This is understood to have been done on the same day on which the earth, at God’s command, brought forth all the fruit-bearing trees; but it is repeated here so that the kind of place paradise is may be known, and because he was going to speak specially of the tree of life and of the knowledge of good and evil.
03_marg233: “And the Lord planted paradise in Eden toward the east,” etc. There are three general views of paradise: one of those who want it understood only bodily; another of those who want it only spiritually; the third of those who take paradise in both ways. I admit that the third pleases me: that man, made from slime, which is the human body, is understood to have been placed in a bodily paradise; as Adam, even if he signifies something else because he is a figure of him who was to come, is taken as a man in his own nature.
03_marg234: The Lord planted paradise in Eden, that is, in delights. Then he sums this up to show how God planted paradise: “And God brought forth from the earth every tree,” etc. For the earth had already then brought forth every tree, namely on the third day. But since the trees set in paradise were of these kinds, he brought forth openly and in their own time those which the earth had already brought forth causally on the third day.
03_marg235: Some copies have “Eden toward the rising.” From which we can gather that paradise is set in the east. But wherever it is, we know that it is earthly, and, with the ocean lying between and mountains set against it, most far removed from our world, set on high, reaching up to the circle of the moon. Whence the waters of the flood did not reach there at all.
03_marg236: Wherein he placed. AUGUSTINE. If anyone thinks that souls stripped of the body are held in bodily places, though they are without a body, there will be no lack of those who agree, and who contend that the thirsting rich man was in a bodily place, and that the soul itself is wholly bodily, because of the parched tongue and the drop longed for from Lazarus’ finger. But it is better to doubt about hidden things than to quarrel about uncertain ones. I do not doubt that the rich man is in torment and the poor man in refreshment. But how the flame of hell, Abraham’s bosom and such things are to be understood is hardly found by the gentle, never by the quarrelsome. But if souls even stripped of bodies are held in bodily places, the thief could have been brought into paradise, where the body of the first man was before. But wisdom is not a body, and therefore not a tree; but it could be signified by a tree. This too I add: that that tree, though bodily, yet gave such food that the body of man was made firm with lasting health, not as from other food but by some hidden breathing-in of healthfulness. For ordinary bread had more power, one cake of which freed a man from hunger for forty days by God.
03_interl196: useful teachings, from which fruit is taken, namely the conduct of the godly
03_interl197: this is wisdom, the mother of all good things
03_interl198: wisdom, which is set in order in the middle, so that it neither claims what it is not nor casts down what it is
03_interl199: by touching which it is known by experience what lies between the good which is left and the evil which follows
03_interl200: that is, the breaking of the commandment
03_marg237: AUGUSTINE. It is said of wisdom: “She is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her.” But there is a Jerusalem eternal in the heavens, and there is a city signifying it founded on earth; Sara and Agar are the two testaments, yet they were two women; and though Christ by the suffering of the wood fills us with spiritual water, yet there was a rock which, struck by a rod, gave water. What was signified was one thing, but they themselves existed bodily; and when they were told it was not figurative speech but the plain telling of things. So there was a tree of life, as the rock was Christ; nor did God will man to live in paradise without mysteries of spiritual things presented bodily. In the other trees there was nourishment; in that, a sacrament. Christ himself too is the sheep which is sacrificed at the pasch, since that was figured not only by saying but also by doing: for it was truly a sheep, it was killed, it was eaten; not like the fatted calf killed for the returning son, for there there is a telling of figures, not a figurative meaning of deeds done. For it is not the evangelist but the Lord who tells it; what the evangelist told also happened, namely that the Lord said such things; the Lord’s telling was a parable, of which it is never required that it be shown according to the letter. Christ is the stone anointed by Jacob and rejected by the builders; but the one was truly done, the other foretold in figure. So wisdom, that is, Christ, is the tree of life in the spiritual paradise, into which he sent the thief from the cross; but a tree of life was created in the bodily paradise, as Scripture says, which tells of things done in their own times.
03_marg238: “The tree of life also,” etc. In the one there was a sign of the obedience which man owed; in the other, a sacrament of the eternal life which he would deserve by obeying. It was called the tree of life because it received from God that whoever ate of it should have his body made firm with lasting health, and should not slip into worse or into decline by any sickness or age.
03_marg239: The tree of life naturally had this power: that whoever ate of its fruit would be clothed with lasting soundness, not to be wearied by any sickness or anxiety or the weariness or weakness of old age.
03_marg240: AUGUSTINE. It was bodily, like the other trees, and not harmful as food; for he who made all things very good set nothing evil in paradise. But the breaking of the command was evil. It was fitting that man, placed under the Lord, should be forbidden something, so that there should be obedience to earn merit, which alone is most truly virtue for the rational creature living under the power of God; just as the first and greatest fault of swelling pride is to will to use one’s own power, which is disobedience. For there would be nothing from which man could think he had a Lord unless something were commanded him. So the tree was not evil, but was called of the knowledge of knowing good and evil, because after the forbidding there would be in it the transgression by which man, by experience, would learn what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Nor was the name given from the fruit which grew on it, but from the thing itself which followed the transgression.
03_marg241: “The tree of knowledge of good and evil.” The middle place and ordered wholeness of the soul is signified. It was planted in the midst of paradise and called of the knowledge of good and evil, because the soul, which ought to stretch toward God, if, forsaking God, it turns to itself and wishes to enjoy its own power without God, learns by experience, as punishment follows, what lies between the good which it forsook and the evil into which it fell; and this will be for it to have tasted of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
03_marg242: And a river went out. BEDE. To water paradise, namely the fair and fruitful trees which adorned all that region, as the Nile waters the plains of Egypt. For God willed that there should be in our world a likeness of the heavenly homeland, which we were created to possess, so as to warn us by a near example to return. But it is agreed that the springs of the rivers which are said to go out of paradise are known in our land: Phison, which is also the Ganges, in the region of Mount Caucasus; Gehon, which is also the Nile, not far from Atlas, which is the spring of Africa toward the west; the Tigris and Euphrates from Armenia. Historians say that the Tigris and Euphrates and the Nile are swallowed up in many places of the earth, and a little later, coming up again, run their usual course.
03_marg243: Another translation: “A spring goes out of Eden, which waters paradise,” etc. These rivers are very well known to the nations through which they flow. Age has changed the names of two: for Gehon is now called the Nile, Phison the Ganges; the Tigris and Euphrates have kept their ancient names. We ought first to take these according to the letter, and not think it only figurative speech, but that they are things and also signify something. But the springs of some are said to be known, of others wholly unknown. So they do not seem, according to the letter, to be divided from one spring, because that place of paradise too, from which they are divided into four parts of waters, is removed from men’s knowledge. But the rivers whose springs are said to be known go under the earth and after long stretches break out where, as at their springs, they are kept from being known, as rivers often do. So a river went out of Eden, that is, out of the place of delights, and watered paradise, namely the fair and fruitful trees.
03_marg244: MYSTICALLY. The river going out of paradise is the overflowing of eternal gladness, of which it is said: “Thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure,” etc. The four rivers are the four cardinal virtues. Phison, which is interpreted “change of mouth,” is prudence, which changes its words to the capacity of its hearers. Whence: “I became all things to all men.” This compasses the land which has the best gold, that is, the discipline of living, refined from earthly dross, which shines into the best gold and is not overcome by falsehood, as the carbuncle is not darkened by night. It has too the appearance of eternal life, which is signified by the greenness of the prasius, because of the greenness which does not wither. Gehon is interpreted “gaping of the earth,” which signifies temperance, which resists unlawful ways; it compasses Ethiopia because it swallows up and consumes foul ways and the kindlings of lust. The Tigris, from its great swiftness, signifies fortitude; it goes against the Assyrians because it carries on untiring action against those who resist the counsels of prudence; for the Assyrians are often put for adversaries, because they often overcame the Israelites. The Euphrates is interpreted “fruitful,” and it is not said against whom it goes, because justice belongs to all the parts of the soul, since it is the order and equity of the soul by which prudence, temperance and fortitude are joined to one another. For it is just that the soul be prudent in contemplating the truth, temperate in reining in desire, brave in bearing adversity.
03_marg245: MORALLY. The earth is watered by four rivers going out of paradise. Prudence, temperance, fortitude and justice hold together the solid building of our reason, because by these four virtues the whole structure of good work rises up. Four rivers water paradise, because while the heart is filled with these four virtues it is cooled from all the heat of fleshly desires.
03_interl210: change of mouth, because it has a meaner face among us than in paradise
03_marg246: A region of India which after the flood was possessed by Hevila, son of Jectan, son of Heber, the patriarch of the Hebrews.
03_marg247: It is interpreted “being in labour,” because one speaking the truth is in labour with it more than he gives birth to it.
03_marg248: He says that the regions of India abound in veins of gold beyond the rest.
03_marg249: According to Pliny it is an aromatic tree the size of an olive, whose tear is clear, bitter to the taste, of a good smell, but more fragrant when steeped in wine.
03_marg250: It is a precious stone, so called because it has a whiteness mixed in it like a human nail, because a nail is called onyx in Greek. The old translation has the carbuncle and the prasius. The carbuncle is of a fiery colour and is said to light up the darkness of night. The prasius is green; whence it took its name in Greek from the leek, which is called prason.
03_interl213: gaping of the earth; this is the Nile, which signifies temperance
03_interl214: namely foul ways and the kindlings of lust
03_interl215: from its great swiftness; this is fortitude
03_interl216: steadfastness against the adversaries of prudence
03_interl217: fruitful, because it makes the land fruit-bearing
03_interl218: fruitful; nor is it said what land it compasses, because it waters the land of promise nearby, and could easily be known by the people who would read these things
03_interl220: so that he might fill the Church from all nations
03_interl221: man, paradise, for pleasure; or God, man, by making him just
03_interl222: man, paradise, so as not to lose it; whence: “Those whom thou gavest me have I kept”
03_marg251: And the Lord God took, etc. AUGUSTINE. He has already said that man was placed in paradise. Now he sums up for what he was placed: “to dress it,” etc. For it is not believable that God condemned him to labour before sin; but we see some farming for pleasure, which was greater then, when nothing adverse befell from heaven or earth. But he had given man the means of working as much as would satisfy his will, not as much as need would force. For the working of providence is twofold: natural and voluntary. Natural, through God’s hidden governing; voluntary, through the working of angels or men. According to the first, shrubs and animals are conceived and born, heavenly and earthly things set in order; according to it come about the things done by an inward and natural movement. According to the other, men teach, learn, farm and the like. In the human body too a natural working goes on, by which the human body naturally comes to be, grows and ages; but by the voluntary it is cared for. The soul too naturally lives and feels; voluntarily it learns and consents. But God creates all creatures good and orders all wills justly. It is believable, then, that man was placed in paradise to work not laboriously but delightfully, and that great and useful things should put the mind of a prudent man in mind. “And to keep it”: that is, perhaps, so that what he did in the earth by farming he should keep in himself by discipline; that as the field obeyed the one who tilled it, so he should obey God commanding, namely that, having received the command, he should yield the fruit of obedience, not the thorns of disobedience. But because he would not, he was condemned and received a field like himself, which yielded thorns and thistles. Or “to keep” paradise, that he should not commit anything for which he ought to be expelled. Whence he received a command too, by keeping which, that is, by observing which, he would not lose it. For he is said not to have kept his property who acts so as to lose it, even if it is safe for others. But above all it is to be said that God should work and keep man himself. Man works the earth, not to make it be earth, but tilled and fruitful; and God works man, whom he created to be man, that he may be just, if he does not depart from him through pride. For “the beginning of the pride of man is to fall off from God.”
03_marg252: In the Morals, book 18. “And the Lord God took man and put him in paradise,” etc. It is to be weighed that good things cannot profit if the evils that creep in are not guarded against; for all that is done perishes unless it is carefully kept in humility. Whence: “to dress it and to keep it,” etc. For he dresses who does the good that is commanded; but he does not keep what he dresses when what is forbidden creeps in. So we must always do good things, and guard ourselves carefully in thought from those very good works, lest, if they lift up the mind, they be not good, since they fight not for their author but for pride. From books too that are not canonical, but put out for edification, we bring a witness: Eleazar, striking an elephant in battle, laid it low, but fell under it. For there are those who overcome vices but, being proud, sink under them.
03_marg253: “And the Lord God took man and put,” etc. For “pleasure,” the Hebrew has Eden. So the Seventy here have now interpreted Eden as pleasure. But Symmachus, who had earlier translated it “a flowering paradise,” here put “delightfulness” or “delights.”
03_marg254: And put him, etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. From what is added, “and to keep it,” it is hinted what kind of working it would be: because in the peace of the blessed life, where there is no death, all working is keeping what you hold. A command was given that they should take of every tree of paradise, but not of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that is, he should not so enjoy it as to break the prohibition by claiming for himself the wholeness of his own nature.
03_interl223: that is, use every virtue for living blessedly
03_marg255: And he commanded him, etc. AUGUSTINE. He was forbidden a tree which was not evil, so that the very keeping of the command should be good for him, and transgression evil. Nor is it better seen how great an evil disobedience is than when man became guilty because, being forbidden, he touched a thing which, had he touched it unforbidden, he would not have sinned. For if, being forbidden, you touch a poisonous herb, punishment follows; and if no one had forbidden it, it would follow likewise. But if a thing is forbidden to be touched which harms not the one touching but the one forbidding, like another’s money, the forbidding is there because it is harmful to the one forbidding. But when a thing is touched which neither harms the one touching if it is not forbidden, nor anyone else if it is touched, why is it forbidden, unless that the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience may be shown by itself? The sinner sought only not to be under God’s lordship, when he committed that from which the command of the Lord alone ought to have dissuaded him, so that God’s will should be set before man’s. The Lord commands; let the servant do what he commands. It is a great profit to man that he serves God, who by commanding makes it profitable. One’s own will lies open to a great fall if, lifting itself up, it sets itself before God’s will. Having experienced this, man learned what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.
03_marg256: It is asked whether he commanded this to the man alone or to the woman too. It is written: “The Lord commanded Adam, saying.” It is not said “he commanded them.” And there is added: “Of every tree of paradise thou shalt eat,” not “ye shall eat”; “but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat”; he did not say “ye shall not eat.” Afterwards he speaks in the plural: “In what day soever thou shalt eat of it, thou shalt die the death.” Perhaps because he was going to make the woman, he so commanded that it should reach the woman through the man. Whence the Apostle: “If they would learn any thing, let them ask their husbands at home.”
03_marg257: “Of every,” etc. If it is asked how he spoke these things, it cannot properly be grasped by us. For it is certain that he speaks either through his own substance or through a creature subject to him. But through his own substance he speaks only for creating all creatures, and for enlightening spiritual ones when they can now grasp the speech which is in the Word of God. But to those who cannot grasp it he speaks through a creature: either a spiritual one, as in ecstasy or in dreams by a likeness of bodily things, or a bodily one too, when he appears to the bodily senses in some form or by a sounding voice. If, then, Adam could grasp the speech of God which he gives the angels through his own substance, he moved his mind for the moment in a wonderful and unspeakable way. But if there was still need of the authority of a holier creature by which he should know God’s command, as for us the prophets and angels, God spoke to him through some creature in words he would understand. And afterwards they heard the voice of God walking in paradise, not through his very substance but through a creature subject to him.
03_marg258: It is asked how they could speak, or understand one speaking, who had not learned it by growing up among speakers or by teaching. But God had made them such that they could speak and learn from others.
03_marg259: It is said of Christ: “Before he know, through good or evil, he shall refuse the evil and choose the good.” How does he either refuse or choose what he does not know? These two are known in one way through the prudence of good, in another through the experience of evil. Through the prudence of good, evil is known and not felt; for one holds to good so that evil is not felt. Through the experience of evil, good is known; for he who has fared badly when the good was lost feels what he has lost. So the child, before he knew by experience the good he would lack or the evil he would feel when the good was lost, refused the evil so as to love the good; that is, he would not lose what he had, so as not to feel, by losing it, what he ought not to lose.
03_interl224: as if: do not corrupt the middle place, by which you are under God and over the creature
03_interl225: of one’s own choice, which is set in the middle for knowing good and evil; whoever, leaving the grace of God, tastes of it shall die the death, deprived of the blessed life
03_marg260: AUGUSTINE. The tree took its name from what followed. For we would not feel evil except by experience, because there would be none had we not done it; for evil is not a nature, but the loss of good is so called. But if they had been obedient and had not sinned against the command, it would still have been called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because this would happen if it were wrongly taken. But they say: how would man understand that the tree was of the knowledge of good and evil, who knew nothing at all of the use of evil? But contraries are known from contraries, as we judge emptiness from fullness and hearing from silence; so from the life that was in him the lack of life, which is now called death, could be known. And the life was sweet which they would avoid losing; nor would sin be urged on them unless it were first said that they would not die of it, that is, would not lose what they loved.
03_marg261: For in what day soever, etc. He does not say “if thou eat, thou shalt be mortal,” but “thou shalt die the death.” For man died in the soul when he sinned, because God, who is the life of the soul, departed from him; which the death of the body followed, the soul, which is the life of the body, departing from it; which happened to Adam when he ended the present life. It can be understood thus: that when they sinned, they were at once punished with that death of which it is said, “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” and elsewhere, “The body indeed is dead because of sin.” He does not say mortal but dead, though mortal because it would die. It is not to be believed that those bodies were so before sin; but though natural, not yet spiritual, yet not dead, that is, such that they must necessarily die, which came about on the day of the transgression.
03_marg262: A twofold death is signified: of the soul, God departing, who is its life; or of the body, which he received at the end of life. But at once he incurred the necessity of dying.
03_interl228: Augustine: perhaps by voices in time; or the very reason was recalled which was in the Word of God first of all
03_interl229: because in the man taken up the Church is joined to God
03_marg263: And the Lord God said, etc. AUGUSTINE. Or perhaps he spoke in the mind of the man himself, as he speaks to certain saints within them, whence: “I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me”; or some revelation was made to the man himself by an angel, either in dreams or in ecstasy or otherwise, as to the prophets; or a voice sounded through a bodily creature, as from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son.” But if we do not know the manner, yet we do not doubt that God spoke. And if he spoke by a bodily voice, or by a likeness of a body expressed in time, he spoke not through his own substance but through a creature subject to him; as he was seen with a head white like wool, and below like fine brass.
