Let us understand, then, what he said: that eternal truth holds that a help like to man was to be made, and in it he hears who can know what was created and why. And the help was to be made for the begetting of children, as the earth is a help to seed, so that a plant may be born of both. Whence: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” etc. This reason for joining did not fail even after sin and punishment, by which the earth is full of men. Sent out of paradise, they came together and begot. But in paradise they could have had honourable marriage and an undefiled bed, without the heat of lust, without the labour of giving birth; not that sons should succeed fathers who were dying, but that, while these remained in some state of form and took vigour from the tree of life, the sons too should be brought to the same state, until, the number being filled, the natural bodies should pass without death into another quality, in which they would wholly serve the ruling spirit and live by the spirit alone giving life, without bodily food. Why then did they not come together in paradise? Because as soon as the woman was created the transgression took place and they were cast out of paradise. For how long a time there was between their being made and Cain’s being born Scripture does not say. Or because God had not yet commanded them to come together, and divine authority could be waited for where desire did not press. But God had not commanded it because he foreknew their fall, from which the mortal human race was to be propagated. But if parents had to give place to children so that a fixed number should be filled by successions, they could, when children were born and the justice of human duty was fulfilled, be carried over to better things not through death but through some change: either that highest one, by which, receiving their bodies, they would become holy like the angels in heaven, or some lower one, by which they would have a better state than this body has; or as the things made before: the man from the slime of the earth, the woman from the man’s flesh. For it is not to be thought that Elias is now as the saints will be when they have received their reward, nor as men who are still living. But if anyone thinks that Elias could not have deserved this if he had taken a wife and begotten children (for he is believed not to have had them, because Scripture did not say so, though it said nothing of celibacy either): Enoch, having begotten sons, pleasing God, did not die but was translated. In the same way Adam and Eve could have been translated. For if Enoch and Elias, dead in Adam and bearing in their flesh the offspring of death, from which they are believed about to return to this life so as to die, are yet now in another life where, before the resurrection of the flesh, before the natural body becomes spiritual, they fail neither by sickness nor by old age, how much more would it be given to the first men, if they had not sinned, that when children were born they should give way to a better state, whence, when the world was ended, they should be changed with all their posterity into the angelic form, not through death but through the power of God. So the woman was made for the sake of begetting, which is not to be taken away. For with God virginity excels, because, since a most plentiful supply is at hand for filling the number of the saints, lust does not claim for itself what the need of receiving offspring no longer requires. Weakness too, prone to a fall into shame, is caught by the honour of marriage; and what is a duty for the healthy is a remedy for the sick. Incontinence indeed is an evil; but marriage, by which the incontinent are joined, is not therefore not good; nor is this good blameworthy because of that evil, but that evil is pardonable because of this good. For the good of marriage cannot be sin, that is, faith, offspring, sacrament. Faith, that there be no coming together with another man or woman, because of the marriage bond; offspring, that it be lovingly received, fed, and brought up religiously; sacrament, that the marriage be not separated, and that the man or woman put away be not joined to another, not even for the sake of offspring. This is the rule of marriage, by which the fruitfulness of nature is adorned and the wickedness of incontinence ruled.
03_marg264: Those who hold that it was not lawful in paradise to come together to beget children perhaps think that all marriage is sin. Those who do not do so, but hold that the fruitfulness of the flesh was given by God for the succession of mortality, do not agree that the first men could have lain together except after sin. But if successors can rightly be sought for those who will die, partners are more rightly sought for those who will live. And they were indeed natural, but would not die had they not sinned, and would receive the angelic form and heavenly quality; when they sinned, a deadly sickness was at once conceived in their members; for even if the body was not yet spiritual but natural, it was not yet of this death, of which and with which we are born. Why then should we not believe that before sin they could command their members of generation for begetting, as the others which the soul has in any work without any trouble or itch of pleasure? Why too should it seem unbelievable that God made such bodies that, had they not sinned, they would command those members as they do their feet, and neither sow with heat nor bring forth with pain? But after sin they deserved the motion of that law which fights against the law of the mind, which marriage orders and continence forbids; so that, as from sin came punishment, so from punishment may come merit. Whoever doubts, then, that the woman was made for the man, from the man, in that sex, in that form and with that distinction of members by which women are known, who bore Cain and Abel, is forced to change all that we believe. And what more just than this punishment: that the body should not serve the soul at its every nod like a servant, as the soul itself would not serve its Lord? Whether both come from the parents, body from body and soul from soul, or the soul is made in some other way.

03_marg265: Brought them, etc. Not as hunters or fowlers do; nor was a voice of command made from a cloud, which rational souls are wont to understand; for beasts and birds do not naturally understand this; but through the ministry of angels, who grasp in his Word what ought to be done and when. For every soul, even the irrational, is moved by commands; but the rational consents or not by the choice of its will; the irrational, which has not this, is driven according to its kind when touched by the command. And when commands are carried out by angels, God’s command reaches not only men, cattle and birds but fishes too, as the whale which swallowed Jonas; and not only these greater ones but even the little worm. It is not said of the fishes that Adam gave them names, but it is believable that, as they were gradually known, names were given according to the difference of nations. But it is to be noted that he did not say “the flying things being formed from the waters,” but from the earth, according to the general use of the word earth by which it is said, “God who made heaven and earth,” etc.; by which whatever was created, whether from the dry land or from the waters, is understood to have been created from the earth.

03_marg268: AUGUSTINE. We must see how the forming of the woman, which is mystically called a building, was done. The angels can create no nature; so neither can they form the rib into a woman, nor the filling of flesh in the place of the rib; not that they do nothing for something to be created, but they are not therefore creators, as neither are farmers of crops or trees. For God alone, that is, the Trinity, is creator. So the woman was made by God, even if the rib was ministered by angels; as a man was made from a woman without any intercourse, when the seed of Abraham was ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator. But it is asked whether the reason which God created together with the first works held that according to it the woman must be made from the man’s side, or only that she could be. But that it should necessarily be done so was not already made there, but hidden in God. The most just course of all nature has natural laws, according to which both the spirit of life, which is created, has its desires bounded in a way which even an evil will cannot pass, and the elements of the bodily world have their fixed force and quality, what each can or cannot do, what can or cannot be made from what. Above this natural course the Creator has it in himself to make from all things something other than their natural reason holds: that a dry rod should suddenly flower and bear fruit, that a woman barren in youth should bear in old age, that an ass should speak, and the like. But God gave natures that these things too could be made from them, not that they should have them in their natural movement. And he has in himself the hidden causes of certain things to come or done, which he did not put into the things made; and he fulfils them not by the work of providence by which natures subsist so as to be, but by that by which he governs as he willed those which he made as he willed. So of all the things which were done to signify grace, not by the natural movement of things but wonderfully, the hidden causes were in God. One of which was that the woman was made from the side of the sleeping man; she was made strong through him, because from his bone; he weak for her sake, because not a rib but flesh was filled in. The first making of things, when it was said on the sixth day, “male and female he created them,” did not hold that the woman should be made so, but that she could be; so that he should not do anything with a changeable will against the causes which he willingly established. So the ecstasy is rightly understood to have been sent for this: that the mind of Adam, sharing in the angelic court and entering the sanctuary of God, should understand the last things. Whence, waking, he uttered with a prophetic spirit: “This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh”; and though Scripture says these words were Adam’s, Christ in the gospel declares that God said them, so that we may understand that through that ecstasy Adam said these things by God’s power.
03_marg269: No faithful just man can be made equal to Christ. For he is “beautiful above the sons of men.” For no one could free the human race except himself. Whence: “No man was found worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof,” etc.
03_marg270: “But for Adam,” etc. The woman was made as a help to the man because there was still something to be done: that not only should the soul rule the body, but also the manly reason should bring under itself its natural part, through which help it commands the body. After the pattern of this the woman was made, whom reason subjected to the man; so that what appears more plainly in two, that is, in male and female, may be considered in one: that the mind should keep subject the desire of the soul through which we work by the bodily members, that is, rule its helper justly. It is shown to man too how far he is above the beasts, which, brought to him, he distinguishes by name and discerns by the judgment of reason. But this understanding is easy; that one harder, by which he understands that the rational which rules is one thing, the natural which is ruled another. In which it is given him to discern irrational movements and, with grace working with him, to bring them under the lordship of reason.

03_marg271: Cast … God, etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. These things cannot be seen with bodily eyes; but the more anyone withdraws, as if falling asleep, from visible things to the secrets of the understanding, the better and more purely he sees. So the very knowledge by which it is known that reason, which commands, is one thing, and the natural part, which obeys, another, is as it were the making of the woman from the man’s rib, to signify their joining. That each may rule this part and become as it were married in himself needs perfect wisdom, whose contemplation is secret and removed from the sense of the body, which is understood by the deep sleep. For then the man is most rightly the head of the woman, when Christ is the head of the man. In the place of the rib he put flesh, not so that flesh should signify fleshly desire, but the affection of love with which each loves his own soul and is not hard so as to despise it; for each loves that over which he is set. So Adam called his wife as the stronger the lesser, and said: “This now is bone of my bones,” etc. Bone of bones because of fortitude, and flesh of flesh because of temperance. These two virtues belong to the lower part of the soul, which rational prudence rules. Whence this part of the soul is called virago, as derived from vir, man. But what follows, “Wherefore a man shall leave father and mother,” etc., is a prophecy to be referred to the sacrament of Christ and the Church.
03_marg272: Those who think that soul comes from soul as flesh from flesh say that God made one soul by breathing into the face of the man, so that from it the others should be created, since Adam was formed first, then Eve. And it has been said whence he had body and soul; but it is not said of her that she was given a soul by God’s breath, as if both were drawn from the man, who already had a soul. But if they think the woman’s soul came from the man’s soul because it is not written that God gave her a soul by breathing, why do they believe she was given a soul from the man, when this too is not written? But if God made all souls as he made the first, Scripture was silent about the others because what was done in one could be understood of the rest. For if something else were done in the woman than in the man, so that the soul should be drawn from flesh that had a soul, and not, as in the man’s case, the body from one source and the soul from another, Scripture ought not to have been silent about what was done otherwise, lest we should think it done as we had already learned. So because it did not say the woman’s soul was made from the man’s soul, it hints that nothing else is to be thought than had been said of the man.
03_marg273: If it is asked whence Christ received his soul, I would rather hear better and more learned men; yet according to my grasp I answer more willingly: not from Adam rather than from Adam. If we say that Levi was in Abraham not according to the soul but only according to the flesh, Christ was there, who according to the flesh is from Abraham, and so he too was tithed. What then is the difference between the priesthood of Christ and the Levitical? Because Levi was tithed by Melchisedech? Unless because it is necessary that in some way Christ was not there. For according to the flesh he was there, according to the soul he was not. So the soul of Christ is not from the stock of the transgression. But it is to be said: although no one’s soul is in his father’s loins according to the flesh, yet in Abraham’s loins Levi was tithed and Christ not tithed, because Levi was there according to the seminal reason, by which reason he would come into his mother through intercourse; according to which Christ’s flesh was not there, although Mary’s flesh was there according to it. For Levi is born of flesh by desire; Christ according to the bodily substance alone. In Abraham was tithed that which was being healed, not that from which it was healed. But if it is said that, as he could be there according to the flesh and not be tithed, so according to the soul: the answer is, if what was said of the flesh could be done with the soul, then the soul of Christ is from the stock in such a way that it did not contract the stain of the transgression. But if it could not be from there without guilt, it is not from there. But as to the other souls, whether they are from the parents or from above, let those prevail who can; I am still moved between the two, sometimes this way and sometimes that. And I would pronounce all the defences of reasons equal or nearly equal on both sides, did not the view of those who think souls are created from the fathers outweigh it on the baptism of little ones, about whom what could be answered has not yet occurred to me.
03_marg274: GREGORY. In the Morals, book 80. “The Lord God cast,” etc. We do not reach the summit of contemplation if we do not cease from the burden of outward care; nor do we gaze on ourselves so as to know that within us the rational which rules is one thing and the natural which is ruled another, unless, running back to the secret place of silence, we are lulled to sleep from outward disturbance. Which Adam sleeping well figured, from whose side the woman soon came forth. For he who is caught up to understand inward things closes his eyes to visible things, and then understands that in himself there is one thing which ought to rule, as the man, another which is to be ruled, as the woman.

03_marg275: And … built, etc. “Wherefore a man shall leave,” etc. ISIDORE. MYSTICALLY. What was fulfilled historically in Adam signifies by prophecy Christ, who left his Father, that is, did not appear to men as he is with the Father; and his mother, that is, the fleshly observance of the synagogue, of which he was born according to the flesh; and clove to his wife, that is, the Church, so that they are two in one flesh; for he is the head of the Church and she his body; who was lulled in the sleep of the passion so that his spouse, that is, the Church, might be formed. Whence: “I have slept and have taken my rest,” etc. So the Church was formed from his side, that is, by faith in the passion and by baptism, because from his side came out blood and water. And he was made of the seed of David according to the flesh, as from the slime of the earth, when there was not a man to till the earth, because no man worked in the virgin of whom Christ was born. A spring rose out of the earth and watered the face of the earth: the face, that is, the dignity of the earth, is the Lord’s mother, whom the Spirit watered so that from such slime that man should be made who was set in paradise, that is, in the will of the Father, to dress and keep it, namely to fulfil and preserve it. For we have received the command in him who said: “As long as you did it to one of these my least, you did it to me.” The tree of paradise signifies spiritual delights; the fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace and the like. We must not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that is, we must not grow proud of the nature which is a middle thing for us, lest, deceived, we experience the difference between good and evil, namely between the Catholic faith and the deceits of heretics. For so we come to the knowledge of good and evil. For “there must be also heresies, that they also who are approved may be made manifest.” For the serpent foreshadows the poisons of the heretics.

03_marg276: AUGUSTINE. If by the words of God or of any prophet something is said which seems absurd according to the letter, and is therefore said figuratively, yet it is not to be doubted that it was said for a meaning. But the bodies of the two people in paradise were naked and they were not ashamed, because they had felt no law in their members fighting against the law of the mind, which followed disobedience. They thought nothing needed covering, because they had felt nothing that needed reining in.
03_marg277: MYSTICALLY. “And they were both naked,” etc. That they were naked and not ashamed signifies simplicity of soul and chastity. Whence: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve, so your minds should be corrupted,” etc. The serpent signifies the devil, who is not simple. Whence there follows: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any of the beasts,” in which his cunning is signified. Paradise is the blessed life, in which the serpent was not, because he was already the devil. That speech is hidden temptation, as he came to Judas persuading him to betray Jesus, since he entered into his heart. But the man who dwells in paradise drives him back; but he is deceived through the woman, because our reason is not led to consent unless delight has been stirred in some part of the soul which ought to obey reason as its ruling husband; nor does anyone slip into sin otherwise. In the serpent is the suggestion; in the woman, lust; the consent of reason, in the man. So desire was stirred; the woman was persuaded. If reason consents to persuading lust, man is driven out of the blessed life as out of paradise, and sin is imputed even if the deed does not follow, because in consenting the conscience is held guilty.
